**HOW TO STUDY THIS MODULE**

Read the module once, without notes, to build the shape of it. Read it a second time with the self-assessment in front of you. Complete the cases only after the second reading. Bring to your mentorship session the one passage you disagreed with.

## The field

*What **private service** is, and what it is not*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Define **private service** and distinguish it, precisely and behaviourally, from hospitality, from the concierge industry, from domestic staffing, and from executive assistance. Situate the profession historically, understand exactly how it collapsed, and understand why it re-emerged in the form it now takes.

Use the vocabulary of the field correctly, from the first day, and understand why the field has several names for one craft.

**1.1 · A definition**

**Private service** is the profession of running the personal life of a wealthy individual or family, from inside their trust rather than inside an institution. It is not a job in an industry with published prices, standard hours and an HR department.

It is a relationship, formalised by a contract, and it lives or dies on a quality that cannot be audited: whether you can be relied upon absolutely.

**DEFINITION**

**Private service**. The direct employment of an individual by a private household or its family office, to manage some part of the principal's personal life, logistics, residences, staff, travel, projects, or the whole of it, under conditions of confidentiality.

The word private is the whole of it. Everything else in your working life so far has been public in some degree: a hotel, a restaurant, a shop, an office. There was a brand between you and the guest, and the brand carried the standard.

Here there is no brand. There is you, and there is a family, and the standard is whatever you personally are.

Attend to three words in that definition, because each one is doing work, and beginners miss all three. The first is direct. You are employed by the family or by the structure the family owns, not by a company that rents you to them.

There is no employer standing between you and the person you serve to absorb a complaint, set your hours, or defend your position. The chain from you to the principal is short and personal, and that shortness is the entire character of the work: it is why the pay is high, why the exposure is total, and why a single failure of trust cannot be appealed to anyone.

The second word is **confidentiality**, and it is not a clause you sign and forget. It is the medium the whole relationship swims in.

The third is the phrase some part of, or the whole of it, because the boundary of your remit is never fixed by the job title; it is fixed by the trust you have accumulated, and it expands and contracts with that trust rather than with any written description.

Understand, from the first hour, what is genuinely being purchased. The principal is not buying labour, which they can hire anywhere and cheaply. They are buying the removal of a category of thought from their own head.

A useful test of whether you have understood the profession at all: when you do your job perfectly, the principal does not think about the thing you handled. Not before, not during, not after. The measure of your work is an absence in their mind, and that is an odd and difficult thing to be paid for, because it is invisible by design and cannot be shown to anyone.

**1.2 · What it is not**

Four professions are routinely confused with this one, including by the people who work in them, and the confusion is expensive. It is expensive because each of the four hires differently, pays differently, rewards different behaviour, and, most dangerously, trains a different set of reflexes.

A person who carries the reflexes of an adjacent field unexamined into a private house will fail in ways they cannot see, because the very instincts that earned them praise elsewhere now read as errors here. So learn the boundaries not as trivia but as a map of the habits you must keep and the habits you must shed.

**Adjacent field.** How it differs, and the behaviour it wrongly trains

**Hotel concierge (Les Clefs d'Or).** Employed by a property, serving many guests, each of them briefly. Rewarded for visible excellence and for the memorable gesture: the upgrade announced with a flourish, the impossible table produced with a smile, the small theatre of being seen to delight. It is genuinely excellent training in resourcefulness, in the black book, in grace under pressure. And it installs precisely the wrong instinct for a private house, because it teaches you to be noticed. The hotel guest leaves in three days and must remember you; the principal stays for years and must be able to forget you. A concierge's warmth is performed and transactional by design, and performance, in a private house, reads as intrusion.

**Concierge company (membership businesses).** A company sells a subscription to a pool of clients and serves them through a rotating team. You serve requests, not a person. The relationship, and the data behind it, belongs to the company, and the client can be handed to a colleague at any moment without loss, because the company, not you, holds the memory of the client's preferences. This is the deepest structural difference from private service, where the relationship is the asset and it is yours: irreplaceable, non-transferable, and destroyed the moment it becomes generic. The membership model trains you to close a ticket. Private service asks you to hold a life.

**Domestic staffing.** Housekeeping, cooking, driving, childcare, gardening. Essential, honourable, highly skilled, and organised around the maintenance of the house rather than the management of a life. A housekeeper is paid for a task done superbly; a house manager is paid for judgement exercised over the whole. It is a different skill on a different ladder, and the two are hired, paid and judged by different measures. This distinction is not a matter of rank or worth. It is a matter of accuracy, and blurring it is how excellent people end up underpaid and misread, described as domestic help when they are in fact running an operation.

A specialist can stand on either side of this line, and the private chef is the clearest case. A chef who runs a principal's whole food life, the sourcing and the suppliers, the dietary discretion, the menus for a table of guests, the food that has to be right on the plane, and who anticipates what the household will want before anyone asks, is doing **private service**.

A cook hired to execute a fixed list of dishes is doing domestic staffing. Same kitchen, different craft.

What places you inside this profession is never the task printed on the label. It is whether you operate inside the family's trust, with **discretion** and judgement over the whole.

**Executive assistance.** Serving a person, as private service does, but in their professional capacity: their diary, their correspondence, their business travel, their office. The boundary between the executive assistant and the private-service professional is genuinely thin, and in this world it is routinely crossed, but in one direction only. The private role absorbs professional tasks far more often than the professional role absorbs private ones, because a life does not divide neatly into work and home, and the person who runs the home is drawn, by proximity and by trust, into everything else. The executive PA who is promoted into the private sphere often finds that the office rhythms of clean hours and defined scope do not survive contact with it, and that the new work has no closing time.

Hold in mind what the four have in common, because it is the thing **private service** lacks and the source of everything difficult about it. In all four, an institution stands between the worker and the person served: a hotel, a company, an agency, a firm.

The institution carries the standard, absorbs the complaint, defines the hours, and can be blamed. Remove the institution, which is exactly what **private service** does, and every one of those functions falls on you alone. That is the field. Everything else in this module is a consequence of that single fact.

**1.3 · A short history, and why it matters**

History is not decoration here. The profession you are entering behaves the way it does, its words, its silences, its manners, for reasons that are a hundred years old, and once you understand where it came from you will stop being surprised by it, and you will stop mistaking its inherited habits for personal eccentricities of the family you serve.

Begin in the old world. The great European household of the nineteenth century, and of the Edwardian years up to 1914, was not a family with some help; it was an institution with a payroll.

A single house might run on thirty, fifty, sometimes a hundred people, with a butler at its head, a housekeeper beside him, and beneath them a codified hierarchy that everyone inside understood without a chart: under-butlers and footmen on the male side, ladies' maids and housemaids on the female, valets, cooks and kitchen maids, grooms and coachmen, gardeners, hall boys, the boot boy at the very bottom.

The two sides of the house were divided by sex and did not mix, and the whole was as ranked as a regiment. It had a career structure as real as any army's: a boy could enter at fourteen cleaning boots and knives in a dark back room and, over forty years of visible **reliability**, rise to run the entire house as butler, dining at the head of the servants' hall while those below him rose in turn.

Service was a life, and often a proud one, entered young and held for a lifetime, and its codes, the discretion, the invisibility, the **anticipation**, the exact register of address, were not invented by anyone. They were refined over generations, the way a craft is, by people who did nothing else.

Much of what you will learn in this programme was first worked out below those stairs, and the reason it still works is that human trust has not changed even though everything around it has.

Then it collapsed, and it is worth knowing exactly how, because nothing about this world is accidental and the shape of the collapse still shapes the field. The First World War took the men to the front, footmen and grooms and hall boys among the first to go, and a great many did not return; the women who had gone into the munitions factories and the offices had tasted a wage of their own and a life outside another family's house, and few chose to come back to service afterward.

Between the wars, death duties and a rising income tax broke the great fortunes, and the great estates with them; houses were shut wing by wing, sold, demolished for their materials, or handed to the nation to escape the tax. There was, famously, a servant problem, discussed endlessly in the newspapers of the 1920s and 1930s: the class that had staffed these houses now had alternatives, factory work, shop work, the growing offices, all with fixed hours and no livery, and having alternatives, it chose them.

The Second World War finished the work the first had begun, and the world that followed, full employment, the welfare state, a new and open suspicion of deference and of the whole idea of being in service, had little room and less appetite for the old arrangement.

By 1960 the profession was widely believed to be finished. The great houses became hotels, schools, corporate headquarters and ruins, and the butler survived in the public imagination mainly as a joke or as a figure in a novel, a relic of a world that had ended.

For a generation it was, in the public mind, genuinely gone. And then, from the 1980s, it returned, and this is the part that concerns you most directly, because it did not return as it had been. It returned changed, and the changes are the daily texture of your job.

A new wealth appeared, on a scale and at a speed the old world had never imagined: the financial deregulation of the 1980s and the fortunes it made in banking and trading, the technology fortunes of the decades that followed, the oil, energy and industrial money of the Gulf and of the former Soviet world, the vast new wealth of Asia and the emerging economies.

It produced a very large, and for the first time genuinely global, population of people who possessed extraordinary means and possessed no inherited system whatsoever for living with them. They had no family tradition of running a great house, no memory of it in their parents or grandparents, and, crucially, they did not want one.

They did not want forty servants in a single country seat, a fixed establishment rooted to one place while they themselves moved constantly.

What they wanted was different, and it defines your job precisely. They wanted mobility: several residences across several countries, aircraft, yachts, a life that moved constantly and could not be run from one place by a fixed staff of forty who never left the estate.

And they wanted, at the centre of that moving life, one exceptional person: a trusted generalist who could make the whole of it work, quietly, carry it in their head, and hold it together as the family moved between cities and continents. For that person, and for the **reliability** that person represents, they were, and are, prepared to pay unusual sums.

The profession answered by professionalising. Specialist agencies appeared to find and vet such people. The family office, borrowed from the way the very rich already managed their money, became the structure through which household staff are hired, paid and managed.

And the language began to shift, deliberately, away from the vocabulary of subservience: from servant toward private professional, from butler toward **estate manager**, house manager, chief of staff. The old titles that survived did so because they carried competence, not because they carried deference.

That is the role you are training for, and its lineage explains its habits. The vocabulary is inherited almost intact from the old world, principal, butler, livery, the household, below stairs, and knowing it will make you sound, from your first interview, as though you belong to the field rather than have merely wandered into it.

But the expectations belong entirely to the new world: speed, mobility, fluency with technology, cross-border logistics, and absolute **discretion** in an age when everything leaks and a single photograph can cross the planet in a minute. You are, in a real and precise sense, a modern profession wearing an old uniform.

Both halves of that sentence carry weight. The old codes give you your register, your restraint and your grace, the things that cannot be improvised and that mark the professional to anyone who can read them. The new demands give you your pace, your tools and your usefulness.

Know only the old, and you are a costume, charming and useless. Know only the new, and you are a fixer without manners, competent and unpolished, whom no serious house will keep near the family. You are asked to be both at once, and that is exactly why the role is rare, and why it is paid as it is.

**1.4 · One craft, several names**

Before anything else practical, a piece of vocabulary that will save you months of confusion, and that almost nobody explains to a newcomer, so that most people discover it slowly and by frustration.

This profession does not have one title. It has five or six, and they describe, very largely, the same craft seen from different angles.

Depending on the house, the country, the size of the operation, and the language of the person writing the advertisement, you will be called a private concierge, a lifestyle manager, a personal assistant, an executive PA, a house manager or an **estate manager**. And the field is wider than those generalist titles suggest.

It also holds the specialists who live inside that same trust, the private chef above all, and other senior household roles, whenever they work with the discretion, the anticipation and the judgement of **private service** rather than as task-workers passing through.

The name on the contract changes with fashion and with circumstance. What you actually do does not change nearly as much as the names suggest: you look after the private life of one family, with discretion, **anticipation** and standards, and you carry the parts of their life they cannot carry themselves.

**The title.** What it usually means, in practice

**Private concierge · Lifestyle manager.** You look after the person. Their time, their travel, their requests, the running of their life outside their work. The purest expression of this craft, and the title most used in the press and in glossy description, though, for that same reason, less used in the agency listings where the work is actually advertised.

**Personal assistant · Executive PA.** The same work, described in the language of the office rather than the house. Calendar, correspondence, travel, personal affairs, the interface between the principal and the world. This is the title you will see most often in an agency listing, and the one you should search for most persistently even when your ambition is a private-service role, because the office vocabulary is where the postings live.

**House manager.** You look after the house. Suppliers, budgets, standards, staff, provisions, the physical running of one residence to a consistent standard whether the family is present or absent.

**Estate manager.** The same craft, at a larger scale and with a wider span. Several residences, real budgets, real teams reporting to you, projects and contractors. A senior step, reached after years, not entered from outside.

**Chief of staff.** Both the person and the operation, across everything: the residences, the office, the staff, the strategy of the private life. The summit of a private-service career, and, correspondingly, rarely reached.

**THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, AND IT MATTERS THIS WEEK**

When you search for a role, search for all of these words, and not only the one that brought you to this academy. An agency will very rarely advertise a private concierge in those words.

It will advertise a personal assistant to a UHNW family, a **house manager**, an executive PA with private duties, a lifestyle and travel manager.@@P@@It is, very often, the same craft, the same kind of house, the same kind of principal, and the same skills you are learning here. The person who searches for only one noun finds almost nothing, concludes that the market is closed to them, and gives up at the very first gate.@@P@@It is not closed.

They were looking for the wrong noun, and the market was full the whole time under a different word.

**1.5 · The vocabulary, from day one**

Use these words correctly from your first conversation, not because the words are magic, but because they are the fastest signal you can send that you already understand the world you are entering. A person who says principal rather than boss, and the office rather than head office, has told the interviewer, in two words, that they will not have to be taught the register.

**Principal.** The person you serve. Never "boss", never "client", never "employer", and never, in the plural loose sense, "the family I work for" when a single word will do. The term signals at once that you know where you are, and it carries the correct professional distance: respect without subservience, closeness without ownership.

**Household.** The residence together with the people who run it, understood as one working entity. Use it when you mean the organisation of a home, and not "the house" when you mean the people and the operation rather than the building.

**The office.** Shorthand for the family office, the private structure that manages the family's affairs and very often employs you. "I'll confirm with the office" is one of the most useful sentences you will ever learn, because it locates a decision correctly, buys you time without evasion, and shows that you understand the chain of authority above you.

**UHNWI.** Ultra-high-net-worth individual, the industry's classification for the tier of wealth these households sit in. Used freely in agency briefs, salary guides and among professionals; never used in front of the principal, to whom it reduces their life to a category and a figure.

**Live-in / live-out.** Whether accommodation is provided on or near the estate as part of the role. It changes the job, the pay, the tax, and the whole shape of your private life, and it is one of the first things to establish about any post, because a live-in role is not a job you leave at the end of the day.

**The schedule.** Still called the rota in older and more traditional houses. The staff roster: who is on duty, who covers, who is off and when. In a serious household it is a written document that everyone can see and rely on, not a loose understanding held in one person's head, and the difference between the two is often the difference between a house that runs and a house that argues.

**Below stairs.** The old collective term for the working parts of the house and the staff who ran them, inherited from the era when the servants' quarters were literally in the basement. You will still hear it, and its modern descendants, "the back of house", "the staff side", used to mean the same thing: the working world of the household as distinct from the family's world above it.

**In private service.** The correct phrase for what you do, and worth preferring over the older "in service", which carries the flavour of the vanished world of deference and can read, to a modern principal, as either quaint or servile. You are in private service, or you are a private professional; you work for a private household. The shift is small and deliberate, and it is the same shift the whole field made when it re-emerged: the competence of the old world kept, the subservience of it set down.

A last point on the words, because it saves a common early embarrassment. This vocabulary is a register, not a costume, and it must fit the house you are in. In an old, traditional English household the full inherited language is expected and reassuring.

In a young technology family that recoils from ceremony, the same language, "the principal", "below stairs", "livery", deployed too thickly, will mark you as stiff and out of place, and you will do better with plainer words and the same underlying discipline. Learn the whole vocabulary so that you always know the correct term.

Then read the house, and use as much of it as the house wants and no more. Knowing the word and choosing not to use it is itself a mark of the professional; not knowing it at all is not.

**1.6 · How the field reads a request**

The clearest way to feel the boundary between **private service** and its four neighbours is to watch the same small request land in each. The words are identical. The reading is not, and the reading is the profession.

Consider a message at six in the morning: "Can someone sort the car for today?" A hotel concierge reads it as a task to be completed visibly and reported back with a flourish: a car booked, a confirmation delivered, perhaps a small upgrade mentioned so the effort is seen.

A concierge-company operator reads it as a ticket: log the request, dispatch it to the driver pool, close it. Domestic staffing reads it narrowly and correctly within its lane: the car needs cleaning or fuelling, so the task is the vehicle itself. The private-service professional reads none of these.

They read a life. "The car for today" is a question about the day, and the day is already known: there is a school run at half past eight, a lunch across town at one, and the usual driver is off. So the reading is not "book a car"; it is "the person who normally makes the morning frictionless is absent, and the principal has noticed a gap they should never have had to notice."

The work is to close the gap and, more importantly, to make sure the gap does not recur, so that the same question is never asked twice. The task-minded neighbour solves the morning. The professional solves the pattern, and says almost nothing about it.

Consider a second, harder in a different way: at six in the morning the principal writes, "Did the Andersons ever send the thing?" No date, no object, no context, and an hour that tells you they woke thinking about it. The hospitality reflex is to ask, and asking is where the amateur reveals himself: Which Andersons?

What thing? By when? Each question is a small tax on a tired mind at an early hour, and four of them together are an insult dressed as diligence.

The field reads the sentence as a compression of something the principal is carrying and would like to set down. The professional's work is to decompress it themselves, from the diary, from the correspondence, from memory, so that the reply is an answer and not another question.

This is the same instinct examined at length later under the service model; note here only that it is a reading, not a technique, and that it grows out of the field's founding fact, which is that no institution stands behind you to define the request. You are the institution, and the institution must already know.

Consider a third, which teaches the boundary with executive assistance directly. Late one evening the principal, between two work matters, says: "While you're at it, can you look at the villa contract for August?" To an executive PA trained in clean scope, this is out of bounds; the villa is personal, the contract is a private matter, and the office assistant would properly route it elsewhere.

The private-service professional understands that in this world the scope is not defined by the title but by the trust, and that a life does not divide itself into work and home for anyone's convenience. The August villa is now yours, because you were the person present and trusted when it surfaced.

The lesson is not that you should absorb every stray task, which is a separate and important discipline of boundaries; it is that the request flowing from the professional to the private sphere, and rarely back, is the structural signature of the field. The person who says "that isn't my department" has told the principal, correctly, that they belong to a neighbouring profession.

Notice what all three readings share. In each, the surface request is trivial and the real work sits beneath it, in a knowledge of the day, the diary, the household and the principal that was built long before the message arrived at six in the morning.

That is the whole of the distinction this chapter has been drawing. The four adjacent fields complete tasks; **private service** holds a life, and a task is only ever the visible edge of it.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

**Private service** is a relationship, not an industry role. It is the direct, confidential employment of a person by a family or its office to run some part, or all, of a private life, with no brand or institution standing between you and the principal to carry the standard or absorb the blame.@@P@@It is not hotel concierge work, not a membership concierge company, not domestic staffing, and not executive assistance, though it borrows from all four and must unlearn the reflexes of each.

The profession is old in its vocabulary and manners and new in its expectations of speed, mobility and technology, and you are judged on both halves at once.@@P@@It travels under five or six different titles that describe one craft, so search for all of them. And its words, principal, the office, household, the schedule, are the first signal a professional sends that they already belong.

## A working taxonomy of wealth

*Because a role at $50M and a role at $2B share a title and nothing else*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Distinguish the tiers of private wealth, and know what each means for your daily work, your reporting line, and your pay. Separate inherited wealth from self-made wealth, and predict how each behaves toward the people who serve it.

Read the difference between liquidity and illiquid assets, and understand why it governs how quickly money moves through your hands.@@P@@Tell a single-principal fortune apart from a multi-generational family, and adjust to the geography and culture the money comes from. Then ask, at interview, the two questions that reveal what the job actually is.

The word wealthy tells you almost nothing. It is the flattest word in this profession, and yet it is the one every job description leans on. A principal worth forty million and a principal worth four billion are both, in the language of the press, simply rich, and the two roles that sit beneath them share a title, a vocabulary, and nothing else at all.

This chapter teaches you to read past the word. You will learn to place a household on a ladder, to trace where its money came from, to understand whether that money is liquid or locked away, and to tell whether you are serving one person or a dynasty.

Read these four things correctly and you will know, before your first morning, roughly what the job is. Read them wrongly and you will spend six months being quietly surprised by a house you could have understood in a week.

**2.1 · The tiers, and why the rung is the job**

Wealth is not a category. It is a ladder, and each rung is a different profession for you. This is not snobbery, and it is not idle taxonomy.

The tier determines who employs you, what you touch in a day, who sits above you, how slowly you are vetted, and what you are paid. A candidate who does not know the tiers will apply to the wrong houses, misjudge their own value, and accept a role whose shape they never troubled to picture. So learn the bands, and learn what each one looks like from the inside.

**HNW · $1M to $30M.** High-net-worth, and the foot of the ladder. One home, perhaps a modest second. Possibly a housekeeper, possibly a nanny, rarely both in any formal arrangement. A concierge here, if the word is used at all, is part-time and blended with three other duties. There is no family office, no chief of staff, no structure above you, because there is nothing yet to structure. The principal does their own admin, or their spouse does. This is not your market, and you should know why: a role here will not teach you the profession, because the profession as this course defines it does not yet exist at this level. It is a household with help, not a household as an operation.

**VHNW and lower UHNW · $30M to $250M.** Very-high-net-worth rising into the ultra tier, and the true classroom of this profession. Two to five residences. A small, real team: a house manager, a housekeeper or two, a nanny, sometimes a chauffeur, occasionally a chef. Travel is private but usually chartered rather than owned. Crucially, the family still decides most things personally, and you will speak to them, or to a spouse, most days. This is where the overwhelming majority of private concierge and lifestyle-manager roles genuinely live, and it is the best place on the entire ladder to learn, because the operation is large enough to be real and small enough that you touch every part of it. You will book the travel and greet the plumber, manage the diary and know the children's shoe sizes. Nothing is yet walled off into a department. Take your first serious role here if you possibly can.

**Upper UHNW · $250M to $1B.** A structured operation, and a different profession. A family office now exists, with its own staff, and it sits between you and the money. Above you sits an estate manager or a chief of staff. Aircraft are owned rather than chartered, and there is often a yacht. Security is a standing function with a director, not a service called when needed. The consequence for you is specialisation: you will not do everything, you will be given a lane, and you will be measured within it. The pay rises and the autonomy narrows. Many people find this trade disappointing after the intimacy of the tier below, and it is worth knowing that in advance.

**Billionaire · $1B and above.** No longer a household but an institution. Dozens of staff, sometimes over a hundred, spread across many properties in many countries. Layers of governance, in-house legal, communications, a philanthropic arm, a serious and permanent security apparatus. Vetting is deep and slow, and it should be, because the exposure is enormous. You may not meet the principal for months. You may serve them faithfully for years and never have a single personal conversation. The compensation is exceptional and the constraint is total: you are one professional inside a system built to run whether any individual stays or goes.

The lesson of the ladder is simple. Ambition tells you to aim for the top rung. The profession tells you that the middle rung, the thirty to two hundred and fifty million band, is where you become good, because it is the only place you will ever be allowed to see the whole of a life at once.

One more thing the tiers teach you, and it is the thing candidates most often get wrong. The bands do not describe how rich someone feels or how they spend; they describe how the household is organised, and organisation is what you are hired into.

A flamboyant principal at the top of the VHNW band may live more visibly than a careful billionaire, but the billionaire's house is an institution and the VHNW house is not, and it is the institution, not the flamboyance, that sets your job. When you read a role, read for structure, not for glamour.

Ask yourself where on the ladder the household sits by counting its homes, its staff, and whether an office stands between the family and the money, and let that, rather than the size of the yacht in the photographs, tell you what the work will be.

**2.2 · Inherited wealth and self-made wealth**

The tier tells you the scale of the house. The next distinction tells you its temperament, and it matters more than scale, because two families of identical wealth can be entirely different employers, and the difference is almost always whether the money was made or inherited.

This is the distinction that separates a practitioner from a beginner, and it is almost never written down. Learn it well.

**Inherited, old wealth.** Money that has passed through two or more generations. It has had time to acquire manners. Its register is restraint: understatement, patina preferred to polish, a quiet horror of anything that announces a price. The house is run for continuity rather than display, and it has a memory. Staff are often long-serving, and there is an inherited model of what staff are and how they are treated, which means the boundaries are already drawn before you arrive. You will be judged on manners before competence, on discretion and calm, and on the sense that you too are built to last. The pay is frequently below market, sometimes markedly so, because old money knows the value of a good reference and expects you to know it too. The tenure is long and the reference, when you have earned it, is gold. The danger is subtle: boredom mistaken for stability, and the slow forgetting that nothing here is urgent, until quietly it is.

**Self-made, new wealth.** Money the principal built and, very often, still controls. It has not had time to acquire manners, and frequently has no wish to. Its register is speed, informality, impatience, and a certain suspicion of ceremony. Decisions are instant and reversed without embarrassment. The pay is good, sometimes excellent, and the expectation is that you will answer at any hour. But there is a specific hazard that inherited wealth almost never presents: because the principal holds no inherited model of what staff are, the boundary between employee and friend erodes. They may treat you as a confidant on Monday and as an employee on Thursday, within the same relationship and without noticing the switch. Old money knows how to be served. New money is learning, sometimes on you. Your task in a self-made house is to supply, gently and without ever saying so, the structure the principal never had time to build.

Hold both pictures side by side and the practical consequence becomes clear. In an old-money house you adapt yourself to a code that already exists, and your risk is complacency. In a new-money house you often build the code yourself, and your risk is boundary collapse. The same competence is required in both. The temperament required is nearly opposite.

**2.3 · Liquidity, and why it lands on your desk**

Here is a distinction the salary guides never mention and the good practitioners never forget: not all wealth moves at the same speed, and the speed at which a family's money moves shapes your working day more than its total ever will.

**Liquid wealth.** Cash, and assets that convert to cash quickly and without loss: public shares, bonds, money in the bank. A family whose fortune is largely liquid can decide something expensive on a Tuesday and act on it the same afternoon. A villa is viewed and offered on Friday. The jet is chartered for Sunday. Requests arrive fast, they arrive fully funded, and they expect you to move at the speed of the money.

**Illiquid wealth.** Value locked inside things that cannot be sold quickly: a private company the principal still owns, property, land, art, a stake in a fund that returns capital on its own slow schedule. A family may be worth a great deal on paper and yet be, in any given month, surprisingly careful about cash. Approvals take longer. Large spends wait for a distribution, a sale, a dividend, a quarter-end.

Why does this matter to you, who will never manage the investments? Because it explains the tempo of approval, and tempo is the thing that catches new professionals out. In a liquid, cash-rich house, when the principal says yes, the money is simply there, and your job is speed and flawless execution.

In an illiquid house, the same yes may be followed by a wait while the office arranges the funds, and if you have committed the family before that machinery has turned, you have created a problem. A founder whose entire fortune is still tied up in the business they are about to sell can look like a billionaire and spend like a careful millionaire until the deal closes, at which point everything changes overnight.

Read the liquidity and you will read the tempo. Learn where the cash actually comes from, how spending is approved, and how long it takes, and you will stop mistaking a slow approval for a lack of trust in you.

Liquidity also tells you something about how a family thinks about money in your presence, which affects how you should speak about it. A liquid, cash-rich house tends to treat spending as a solved problem: the answer to cost is usually simply arrange it, and to labour the price of a thing is to waste the principal's attention.

An illiquid or asset-heavy family, even a very grand one, often carries a genuine consciousness of cash flow, and here a well-timed note that a spend can wait for the next quarter, or that a supplier will hold the price for a month, is heard as competence rather than penny-pinching.

You are not being asked to have opinions on the family's finances, which would be a serious overstep. You are being asked to notice whether cash is abundant and instant or valuable and scheduled, and to pitch your handling of money to match.

Reading this correctly is one of the quiet marks of a professional, and misreading it, spending freely in a house that watches its cash, or fussing over cost in a house that finds fuss tiresome, is a small error that accumulates into a reputation.

**2.4 · One principal, or a dynasty**

The last structural reading is the number of people the wealth belongs to, and it changes almost everything about the politics of your role.

**The single-principal fortune.** One person made the money and one person, or one couple, controls it. The chain of command is short and it terminates in a human being you can, in principle, reach. Decisions are fast because they are personal. The household reflects a single temperament, and once you have read that temperament you have read the house. The risk is precisely that everything runs through one person: their mood is the weather, their attention is the budget, and when they are distracted the whole operation waits. You serve a person, and you succeed by understanding that person deeply.

**The multi-generational family.** The money belongs to a family, often across three or four living generations, and no single person simply decides. There are parents and adult children, in-laws and trustees, a matriarch or patriarch whose word still carries even when their name is off the accounts. There are branches of the family that do not entirely agree, and a family office whose real job is to keep the peace between them. Here you do not serve a temperament, you serve a system, and the system has a politics that predates you by decades. The senior generation may value one thing and the next generation another, and you will be caught between them over something small. Your skill is not reading a single person but reading a constellation: who truly holds authority, who merely holds a title, and whose quiet objection can stop a thing the nominal head has approved. The single-principal house rewards intimacy. The dynastic house rewards diplomacy, patience, and an unfailing refusal to be seen taking a side.

There is a moment in the life of a dynastic family that you should learn to recognise from the outside, because it will define your experience if you are inside it: the succession. Wealth that is passing from a founding or senior generation to the next is wealth in motion, and the household around it becomes tense, political, and prone to sudden change.

Loyalties that were settled for twenty years are suddenly in play. The staff who served the patriarch may be uncertain whether they will suit the son who is taking over, and the son may wish to remake the household in his own image.

If you join a family in this phase, understand that you are joining a negotiation, and that competence alone will not protect you; you must be visibly useful to the generation that is arriving, not only loyal to the one that is leaving.

Read whether a family is settled or in transition, and you will understand why a house that looks calm on paper feels, from within, as though the ground is moving.

**2.5 · Where the money was made, and how the house runs**

Wealth has a geography and a culture, and the same fortune runs a very different household depending on where and how it was made. You will meet these archetypes within your first week, and reading the wrong one is how a strong candidate loses a strong post. Learn them as living patterns, not stereotypes: every family bends the mould, but the mould is real.

**Old European money.** The great estates and dynastic families of Britain and the Continent. The register is continuity and understatement, discussed above, expressed here through institutions: the family seat, the long-serving butler or house manager, the family office that behaves as a patient steward rather than a startup. Hierarchy is settled and quiet. Codes are everything, and they are never explained, because everyone who belongs is assumed to know them already. You are judged on whether you, too, seem built to last. Show restraint, learn the codes by watching, and never mistake the absence of drama for the absence of standards.

**United States technology and finance.** Two distinct cultures under one flag, and you must not confuse them. Technology fortunes are made fast and often young. The register is informality and optimisation: flat structures, first names, a suspicion of ceremony, an appetite for anything that removes friction, and, alongside it, an intense, almost paranoid concern with privacy and data. Expect severe NDAs, device and messaging policies, and a distaste for anything that looks like ceremony or hierarchy. Finance money, by contrast, is made in banking, private equity, hedge funds, and trading, and its register is performance: process, metrics, reporting, short briefings, explicit standards, mistakes noticed at once. Tech wants its life engineered and its hierarchy invisible; finance wants a system and is pleased when you build one. Both pay well. Tech will erode your boundaries through informality; finance will hold professional distance and, in a bad quarter, replace you in an afternoon.

**The Gulf, and the great resource fortunes.** The households of the GCC, and the oil, energy and industrial families of the region and beyond. The register is scale, hospitality, and protocol. Households are large, family and guests are near-constant, and the calendar is seasonal in its own way: the summer abroad to escape the heat, the return, the holy days that govern everything. Hierarchy is strict and intricate, gender-segregated staffing is the norm in some houses, and discretion is not a preference but a cultural and often legal absolute. The packages are generous, sometimes extraordinarily so, and the environment is formal and demanding. You are expected to understand religious and cultural observance without being told, and above all to read the web of family and rank precisely, because authority does not always sit where a Western eye expects it to. The danger is misreading the hierarchy. The cure is patience: watch, learn who truly holds authority, and never assume it maps neatly onto a title.

**Asian family conglomerates.** The dynastic business families of East and South Asia, whose wealth sits inside a group of companies passed down and run by the family. The register is structure, hierarchy, and a deep sense of the family as an institution. Seniority and generational respect are load-bearing, not decorative. The household and the business are often intertwined, the family office may be indistinguishable from the group's head office, and decisions can move through a family council rather than a single desk. Face and propriety matter, obligations run in both directions, and long service is honoured. Read the generational lines carefully, defer correctly, and understand that here, more than almost anywhere, the newcomer earns standing slowly and by conduct.

**Entertainment, sport, and public life.** Fame rather than accumulated wealth, and image and security above all else. The register is speed, exposure, and constant management of a life lived partly in public. Calendars are chaotic, the entourage is large and its loyalties are unclear, and discretion is tested weekly rather than yearly. Tenure is short and the single greatest professional risk in the whole field, the leak, sits here, because you are surrounded by people who can monetise access. In this world discretion is not one virtue among several. It is the entire job.

**Emerging-market and recently mobile fortunes.** The very large fortunes of Russia, Eastern Europe, Latin America, and the fast-growing economies, frequently made in a single generation and often held by families who have relocated their lives, and sometimes their safety, across borders. The register combines the speed and personal control of self-made wealth with an acute concern for security, discretion, and the loyalty of those around them, because the wealth was built in environments where trust was scarce and exposure was dangerous. Households can be generous and warm and, at the same time, watchful; the inner circle is small and closes ranks quickly. Here you earn your place by proving, over time, that you are reliable and silent, and you do not expect the easy informality that a Californian founder might offer in the first week. Patience and evident discretion are the currency.

Notice that these cultures cut across the tiers and across the inherited-versus-made line: there is old money and new money in every geography, liquid and illiquid fortunes in each. A Gulf family may be dynastic and asset-rich; a US tech founder may be single-principal and dazzlingly liquid; an Asian conglomerate family may be multi-generational and, on paper, largely illiquid.

Use geography as a fourth lens, laid over the first three, and your reading of a house becomes genuinely three-dimensional. No single lens is sufficient, and the practitioner who relies on one, who assumes all new money behaves alike, or that all Gulf houses are the same house, is the practitioner who is repeatedly surprised.

**2.6 · Reading the type, and changing what you do**

Taxonomy is worthless until it changes your behaviour. Here are four short illustrations of how reading the wealth type alters the actual work, on an ordinary day, in a way a colleague who reads only the job title never manages.

Consider the same request, "book us somewhere nice for Saturday", arriving in two houses. In the old-money house you choose the quiet, established table the family has used for years, you confirm it without a word about cost, and you never mention that it was fully booked when you called.

In the new-money founder's house you send two options with a line on why each is interesting, you move fast, and you expect the plan to change twice before Saturday. Same words, two entirely different professionals answering them, and the difference is your reading of the register.

Consider a five-figure spend, a case of wine, a piece of garden furniture, a deposit on a rental. In a liquid, cash-rich finance household you place it, log it cleanly, and report it in your monthly summary, and speed is the virtue.

In an illiquid house whose founder's wealth is locked in a business not yet sold, you route the same spend through the office for approval first, because committing the family before the cash is arranged is precisely the error that plants doubt. The competence is identical.

The sequence is opposite, and you chose the sequence by reading the liquidity.

Consider an instruction from an adult son in a multi-generational Asian family conglomerate that appears to contradict a standing arrangement set by his father. In a single-principal house you would simply act on the instruction of the person who employs you.

Here you do not: you recognise that authority runs through the senior generation, you confirm quietly with the office or the person who holds the elder's confidence, and you avoid being the instrument of a family disagreement.

Reading the structure, one principal or a dynasty, told you not to move at the speed the words invited.

Consider a supplier who telephones to ask, pleasantly, when the family will next be away so he can schedule the works. In most houses this is a scheduling question. In an entertainment or public-life household, or any house with real security exposure, it is a red flag, and you give nothing, route it through security, and note who asked.

The type of household turned an innocent question into a test, and you passed it only because you had read the house.

** IN PRACTICE**

Before your first day in any post, place the house on all four readings at once. Which tier: what scale of operation, and will you touch everything or a single lane?

Made or inherited: do you adapt to a code that exists, or build one that does not?@@P@@Liquid or illiquid: does yes mean now, or yes mean when the funds arrive? One principal or a dynasty: do you serve a temperament, or navigate a constellation?

Then lay the geography over the top.@@P@@Five minutes of this, done honestly, will tell you more about the job than any brief the agency sends you.

**2.7 · The two questions**

All of the above can be approximated, before you accept anything, from two questions you are entitled to ask at interview and should never leave the room without asking. They are not impertinent. They are the questions a professional asks, and asking them is itself a signal that you understand the field.

**ASK, ALWAYS**

"How many residences?" This one number reveals the true scale of the work, the volume of travel, the complexity of the logistics, and, indirectly, the tier. "How many staff, and to whom would I report?"@@P@@This reveals whether you are the operation or a part of it, and it draws the chain of command before you are inside it, which is to say before it can be used against you.

Two numbers and one name. Between them they describe the job more accurately than any job description you will ever be sent, and a candidate who asks them calmly is a candidate who has clearly done this before, even when they have not.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

The tier of wealth shapes the job more than the job title does, and the thirty to two hundred and fifty million band, where the family still decides personally and you still touch everything, is the finest classroom in the profession. Whether a fortune was inherited or made predicts the culture: old money hands you a code to adapt to and risks your complacency; new money asks you to build the code and risks your boundaries.@@P@@Liquidity sets the tempo of approval, and mistaking a slow, illiquid approval for distrust is a beginner's error.

A single-principal house rewards intimacy with one temperament; a multi-generational family demands diplomacy across a constellation. Geography adds a fourth lens: old European restraint, US tech privacy and finance performance, Gulf scale and protocol, Asian generational hierarchy, and the exposure of public life.@@P@@Read all four at once, and two questions at interview, residences and staff, let you do it before you ever accept the role.

## The family office

*The chain of command, and how it breaks*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Describe the structure of a single-family and a multi-family office, and name the roles inside it. Locate yourself in the reporting line, and know precisely who hires you, who reviews you, and who pays you.

Identify who signs, who decides, and whose trust must be won.@@P@@Handle a contradiction between the principal and the office without being blamed by either, and understand how information is meant to move through the structure and where it must not.

**3.1 · What it is**

**DEFINITION**

Family office. A private structure established to manage the wealth and affairs of one family (a single-family office, SFO) or several (a multi-family office, MFO). Its remit typically includes investments, tax, legal, property, philanthropy, insurance, and, critically for you, the employment, payroll and contracts of household staff.

Above roughly a quarter of a billion, a family ceases to be a household and becomes an organization with a head office. This is not a metaphor. There is a legal entity, or several; there are employees who have never set foot in the residence; there is a payroll run, an accounts department, a set of policies, and a governance structure that meets on a schedule.

You have not been hired by a person. You have been hired by an institution that happens to be owned by a person, and the two behave very differently.

The consequences for you are immediate and practical. The person who interviews you may not be the person you serve. The person who signs your contract is rarely the person whose trust you must win.

The instruction you receive at nine in the morning from one may be reversed at three in the afternoon by another. And the pay slip that arrives at the end of the month comes not from the family whose life you run but from an entity with a name you may not recognise, in a jurisdiction you may never visit.

None of this is sinister. It is simply the architecture of managed wealth, and the professional who understands the architecture moves through it without friction, while the one who does not spends years puzzled by things that were never puzzling to anyone who could read the chart.

**3.2 · Single-family and multi-family offices**

Not every family office is the same animal, and the difference changes your job before your first day.

**DEFINITION**

Single-family office (SFO). A private organisation set up to serve one family exclusively: its investments, taxes, philanthropy, property, and often its staff.

Hired through an SFO, you serve one principal, your reporting line is comparatively clear, and the whole attention of the office is fixed on that one family.@@P@@The people in it are, in effect, that family's private civil service. They will come to know you, your house and your habits intimately, for better and for worse.

**DEFINITION**

Multi-family office (MFO). A firm that serves several wealthy families at once, sharing professional infrastructure, investment expertise, accounting, legal and administrative capacity, across all of them.

Placed or managed through an MFO, you may be one of many household staff it oversees on behalf of many different principals.@@P@@The relationship is more arms-length and more procedural; your day-to-day principal is still the family, but the structure behind them is shared, and the person who administers your contract may be administering forty others for a dozen families they see as accounts.

The practical differences run deeper than the definitions suggest, and you should learn to read them at once.

- Loyalty and knowledge. An SFO knows one house completely.

An MFO knows a little about many, and treats yours as one file among many. In the SFO, a five-year memory of the family's preferences sits in the room with you.

In the MFO, it may not exist at all, because the firm's memory is organised around money, not around the family's dinner habits.
- Professionalism and distance. The MFO is usually more procedural, more documented, more like a professional firm, because it must be, it serves many masters and cannot improvise for each.

The SFO can be warmer and more personal, and also more political, more prone to favouritism, and more vulnerable to the moods of a single dominant individual.
- Who truly decides. In an SFO, real authority often sits close to the principal, sometimes in a single trusted lieutenant.

In an MFO, authority over your affairs is more diffuse and more rule-bound; you will be told "that is our policy" far more often than "the family prefers".

Know which you are dealing with before you accept the role, because it tells you how personal the loyalty beneath the arrangement really runs, and therefore how much of your security rests on relationships and how much on paperwork. In the SFO, protect the relationships. In the MFO, protect the paperwork. In both, do both.

**3.3 · Who is who inside the office**

An office of any size has a set of functions, and though the titles shift from house to house and country to country, the functions do not. You will not deal with all of these people equally. Some you will speak to weekly; some you may never meet.

Learn the whole map anyway, because the ones you never meet are frequently the ones who decide your fate.

**Function.** What they control, and what it means for you

**Principal.** The owner of the wealth and, ultimately, of you. In a family office structure the principal sets direction and delegates administration; they are not usually the person you go to with an invoice or a rota. You serve them and you rarely deal with them on operational matters, and when you do, it is significant, and you treat it accordingly.

**Family office principal, CEO, or director.** The professional head of the office, often a former private banker, lawyer, or senior executive brought in to run the family's affairs. They own strategy and governance for the whole structure. You will rarely deal with them directly. When you are summoned to them, something has gone right enough to be noticed or wrong enough to matter.

**Chief investment officer (CIO).** Runs the money: the portfolio, the managers, the investment strategy. This person is the reason the office exists, and consumes most of its attention and its status. For your purposes they are almost entirely irrelevant to daily work, and it is useful to know that, because it tells you where the office's centre of gravity truly sits, and it is not on you. The household is a cost centre in a building organised around an investment engine. Understanding that keeps you humble and keeps your reporting tidy.

**Chief financial officer, controller, or head of finance.** Payroll, expenses, budget approval, the accounts. Your monthly household reporting goes here. This is one of the two or three people you will actually deal with constantly, and they will judge you not on charm but on tidiness: reconciled figures, receipts that match, budgets that hold, explanations that arrive before they are requested. They speak to everyone, and their quiet opinion of you travels further than you think.

**Function.** What they control, and what it means for you

**Chief of staff.** Where one exists, this is very often your true line manager, the person to whom the running of the family's personal life is delegated. They own the operation as the CEO owns the investments. Win them and you are secure. Bypass them, even once, even for a good reason, and you are finished, because you will have demonstrated the one thing they cannot tolerate, that you will go around them when it suits you.

**Estate director, or director of residences.** Where the portfolio of properties is large enough to warrant it, this role sits between the office and the houses, owning properties, capital projects, budgets and major vendors across all of them. Your work passes across their desk constantly. In smaller structures this function is folded into the chief of staff or handled by you directly.

**General counsel, or legal.** Contracts, non-disclosure agreements, employment matters, incidents, disputes, immigration and visas for staff. If you ever genuinely need counsel, you need them urgently and you need them right, and knowing when a situation has become legal rather than practical, an accident, an allegation, a dismissal, a press enquiry, is itself a senior professional skill. Escalating too early wastes their time; escalating too late can cost the family a great deal, and cost you the role.

**Head of security.** Movements, vetting, guest clearance, residences, travel, threat assessment. Nothing you plan happens without them, and you will meet the discipline of this function in detail later in the programme. For now, understand that they sit inside the office structure as a standing department, not as a service you hire, and that their authority over certain decisions simply exceeds yours.

**Executive and personal assistants to the principal.** These are office-side assistants who manage the principal's diary, correspondence and professional life from within the structure. They are not household staff, and the distinction matters: they sit closer to the principal's daily attention than almost anyone, and a great deal of what reaches you will reach you through them. Treat the principal's EA as a peer to be cultivated, never as a subordinate to be instructed, whatever the apparent seniority of your own title.

Notice which of these you will actually deal with. In practice, day to day, it is a short list: the chief of staff or estate director above you, the controller for money, the principal's EA for the diary, and security when movements are involved.

The CIO, the CEO and counsel exist at the edge of your working life, and the skill is knowing they are there, knowing what they control, and knowing the moment a matter crosses into their territory.

**3.4 · Where you sit, and how the line runs**

The single most important thing to establish in your first week is the shape of the line above you, because a household staff member almost never reports directly to the principal in a family office structure. There is something in between, and you must know exactly what.

Read the structure from the top down. The principal sits at the summit, but delegates. Below the principal, the office administers: the CEO runs the whole, the chief of staff or estate director runs the personal and residential side of it, and the household, your world, hangs beneath that.

You are, in organisational terms, at the bottom of the office chart and the top of the house chart at once, and that double position is the whole peculiarity of the role. Below you sit the residence staff, the housekeepers, the drivers, the chef; above you sits the office.

You are the hinge between the two, translating the family's life into instructions the house can execute, and the house's reality into reporting the office can trust.

This means, in almost every case:

- You are hired by the office, not by the family, even when the family interviews you last and decides.
- You report to a manager in the office, the chief of staff or estate director, not to the principal, for operational matters.
- You are reviewed and paid through the office, on its calendar and by its rules.
- And yet you are judged, ultimately and privately, by the family, whose verdict the office will follow.

Hold both halves of that at once. Your line manager can protect you or expose you, and the family's regard is what finally decides, and the two do not always agree. The professional keeps both satisfied. The naive one serves whichever spoke to them last.

**3.5 · How you are hired, onboarded, reviewed and paid**

Because the office is an institution, the whole employment relationship runs on institutional rails, and you should understand each stage before you are inside it.

**Hiring.** The role usually reaches you through a specialist agency, which the office has retained. You are screened by the agency, then interviewed by the office, the chief of staff or estate director, sometimes the controller or a security representative, and only then, if at all, by the principal or their spouse. The offer, the contract, the salary and the terms come from the office. The family's role is frequently to say yes or no at the end, on the strength of a single meeting and their instinct in it. Understand from this that you are being sold twice: to the office on competence, and to the family on character, and the two audiences want different things.

**Onboarding.** In a serious structure you will be given a contract, a job description, an NDA of real severity, a set of policies, and access to systems, expense cards, calendars, contact lists, sometimes a household manual. In a weaker structure you will be given a set of keys and a vague sentence, and left to invent the system yourself, which is both a burden and an opportunity. Establish in the first week, in writing, three things: your reporting line, your spending authority, and your confidentiality obligations. Ask for them plainly. A well-run office will respect the question; a badly run one needs it asked even more.

**Review.** You will be appraised on the office's cycle, annually in most structures, by your line manager, not by the principal. The family's view feeds in from above and is rarely quoted to you directly. This is why so much of your standing rests on the relationship with the chief of staff or estate director: they write the review, they set the bonus recommendation, and they carry the family's murmurs into a formal record you never see.

**Pay.** You are paid by the office entity, through its payroll, in its jurisdiction, on its schedule. Salary is set and adjusted by the office. The bonus, discretionary in nearly every house, is recommended by your manager and approved above. Never treat the principal as your paymaster, and never, ever raise money with the principal directly. The moment you discuss your own compensation with the family rather than the office, you have stepped out of your position and into theirs, and you will be gently but permanently marked as someone who does not understand the structure.

**3.6 · Who runs the household, the office or the house**

Two models exist, and your authority depends entirely on which one you are in.

In the first, the office runs the household directly. It hires the staff, holds the budgets, sets the systems, and the **house manager** reports into it and executes. Here you propose, and the office decides.

In the second, the office handles only money and affairs, and delegates the running of the residences to a senior household professional, which is to say, to you. Here you decide, within a budget, and then inform. Most real situations sit somewhere between, with a threshold: below a certain sum or significance you act and report; above it, you ask.

Establish that threshold early and precisely, because misreading it is one of the fastest ways to damage yourself. Act as though you decide when in fact the office decides, and you will be resented as someone who oversteps. Act as though you must ask when the office expected you to run the house, and you will be thought weak, a manager who cannot manage.

The threshold is rarely written down in useful detail, so you infer it, test it with small cases, and confirm it in writing the moment you have it.

**3.7 · The three questions of your first week**

Answer these before you attempt anything ambitious. They are not administrative details. They are the political map of your working life, and everything you do sits on top of them.

- Who signs? Contracts, invoices, budget approvals, new hires, changes of supplier.

In a family office structure this is almost always the office, and often a specific named person, the controller for money, the chief of staff for people. Learn the exact chain, cold, and never improvise it to save a step.

The professional who moves money cleanly through the right hands every time, and can explain any figure the same day, is trusted with more. The one who routes a payment the wrong way to be helpful plants precisely the doubt that ends careers.
- Who decides?

On the day, in the house, on the things that cannot wait for a meeting. Often the principal; often a spouse; sometimes a personal assistant of fifteen years whom no one thought to put on the chart but whose word is treated as the family's own.
- Whose trust must I win?

Frequently a third person entirely, neither the signer nor the obvious decider, and it is the answer to this question that quietly determines whether you are still in the role in two years.

Keep these three separate in your mind at all times. The classic early error is to collapse them, to assume the person who signs also decides, or that winning the decider is the same as winning the office. They are three different people with three different powers, and confusing them is how competent newcomers make enemies they cannot name.

**3.8 · Confidentiality and the flow of information**

The office is not only a management structure. It is an information structure, and your position inside it carries strict rules about what moves where.

The principle is compartmentalisation. Information travels on a need-to-know basis, and your job is to move each fact to exactly the people who need it and no further. The controller needs the household's numbers; the controller does not need to know the contents of a private conversation you overheard.

Security needs the travel dates; the chef does not need to know the reason for the trip. You will hold, in the ordinary course of your work, a great deal that has no business travelling at all: the family's whereabouts, their disputes, their health, their guests, their finances.

The NDA you signed is the legal floor of your **discretion**, never its ceiling, and the office will judge you constantly, if silently, on whether you understand the difference between reporting and gossip.

Two disciplines follow, and you should adopt both from the first day.

- Report upward, never sideways or downward, on anything sensitive. A concern about the family goes to your line manager in the office, in a measured written note, not to a colleague over the staff meal and not to the principal in passing.

The office is built to receive difficult information cleanly; the staff room is built to amplify it.
- Assume everything you write is permanent and discoverable. Messages, emails, notes, expense memos: write each as though it may one day be read by the principal, by counsel, or in a dispute, because any of them may.

This is not paranoia. It is simply the standard of a house where a single careless line can migrate into a place it was never meant to go.

**3.9 · The contradiction, and the sentence that saves you**

This is the most common structural failure in the profession, and it destroys perfectly competent people. It arises directly from the double line you now understand: the family above you personally, the office above you formally.

The principal asks you for something. The office refuses it, or would refuse it if asked, because it breaks a budget, a policy, or a plan the family cannot see. Both consider themselves final, and in a sense both are.

You are in the middle, and whichever way you move, you are wrong. If you obey the principal, you have gone around the office and broken the structure. If you obey the office, you have refused the family.

You do not choose a side. You do not quietly proceed and hope it is never noticed. And you do not carry back to the principal the news that the office has refused them, because that is not your message to carry, and delivering it makes you the visible face of a refusal that is not yours.

**THE SENTENCE**

To the office: "The principal has asked me for this. I want to make sure it is handled correctly.

How would you like me to proceed?"@@P@@You have now returned the decision to the people whose decision it is, and you have made yourself the person who handles things correctly rather than the person who caused a problem. Both are true, and both are visible.

The office resolves the matter upward if it must, the principal receives whatever answer the structure produces, and your name is attached to neither the request nor the refusal, only to the competence.@@P@@The staff member who resolves this alone, by guessing, is blamed by both sides. Always, and without exception.

**3.10 · Two illustrations**

Consider first a single-family office of moderate size. The principal, at breakfast, mentions to you that they would like the pool house at the country estate refitted before the summer, and to "just get it done".

You know, because you have read the structure, that a capital project of that scale is signed by the estate director and budgeted by the controller, and that the principal's breakfast wish is a direction, not an authorisation.

The beginner rings a contractor that afternoon and starts a project the office has neither costed nor approved, and is later found to have committed the family to a six-figure sum no one sanctioned. The professional says, warmly, "Of course, I'll get it moving straight away," and then takes the wish to the estate director the same morning: "The principal would like the pool house done before summer.

Shall I get three quotes together for you to approve?" The wish is honoured, the structure is respected, the project happens, and the professional is the person who made it happen correctly.

Consider second an arrangement through a multi-family office. Your principal asks you to advance a payment to a supplier a week early as a favour. You raise it with the MFO's finance contact, who administers a dozen families and replies that the firm's policy does not permit early release without a sign-off you cannot obtain in time.

Here the discipline is the paperwork, not the relationship, because in an MFO the relationship is thin. You do not lean on a personal bond that does not exist; you return to the office with the constraint and a solution: "Finance can't release early under policy, but I can confirm the payment for the standard date and let the supplier know it's guaranteed, would that hold them?"

You have served the principal's real need, the supplier's confidence, without breaking a rule that would have exposed you in a structure that runs on rules.

Consider, finally, the quiet case that never becomes a story. Over several weeks you notice the household's monthly figures drifting above budget, small overruns, nothing dramatic. You do not wait to be asked, and you do not raise it with the family.

You send the controller a short written note before the quarter closes, setting out the drift, the cause, and two ways to bring it back. The controller, who speaks to everyone, files you privately as the kind of manager who surfaces a problem while it is still small.

That note, unremarkable in itself, is worth more to your standing than a year of flawless dinners, because it tells the office the one thing it most wants to know about anyone who holds its money: that you report before you are caught, not after.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

Above roughly a quarter of a billion, a family office sits between you and the family, an institution with its own executives, its own money side, and its own rules. A single-family office knows your house intimately and runs on relationships; a multi-family office is procedural and distant and runs on paperwork.@@P@@You are hired, onboarded, reviewed and paid by the office, not the family, and you report to a manager, usually a chief of staff or estate director, while the family's private verdict decides your fate from above.

Signing, deciding and trusting are three different people; confusing them is the classic early error.@@P@@Information moves upward and on a need-to-know basis, never sideways into the staff room. And a contradiction between the house and the office is escalated, calmly and in writing, with the sentence that returns the decision to those whose decision it is, never resolved by guesswork.

## The household as an organization

*Functions, departments, and how the work actually flows through a home*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

See a great household as a small organization rather than a house with staff in it. Name its functions and describe how they coordinate.

Understand the role of written standards, the house book, and the daily rhythms that keep a home, or several homes, moving in step.@@P@@Recognize the organizational failures that undo competent people, and position yourself, as a newcomer, without provoking those who can end you.

**4.1 · A house is an organization, and you must learn to see it as one**

Most people who enter this profession see a home. You must learn to see something else underneath it: an organization, small but complete, with functions, departments, a chain of command, a budget, standards, and a flow of work that either runs smoothly or does not.

The furniture and the flowers are the surface. Beneath them is an operation, and your value is decided almost entirely by how well you read and run that operation, not by how the drawing room looks to a guest.

This is the shift the whole chapter asks of you. A restaurant, a hotel, a shop, these are organizations that everyone recognizes as such, with departments and rotas and a manager. A private home at this level is exactly the same kind of thing, and almost nobody names it.

The family will not call it an organization. They will call it home, and they will expect it to feel like one. But a principal residence with eight staff, a chef, a driver, a nanny and a security detail is a small enterprise, and a portfolio of four homes with thirty people across them is a genuine company that happens to have no logo and no published accounts.

**DEFINITION**

The household as an organization. The whole coordinated operation that runs a principal's private life across one or more residences: its functions, its staff, its suppliers, its standards, and its budgets, held together by a chain of command and a set of shared routines.
