- Capture now, not later. Photograph the receipt the moment it is handed to you and log it the same day: amount, category, purpose, and which card or float paid it. An expense reconstructed from memory a month later is both inaccurate and unconvincing, and it reads as exactly what it is.
- Where a supplier gives no receipt, ask for one; where none exists, write your own contemporaneous note, dated, before you leave the premises. A note made on the day is evidence. A note made at month end is a story.
- Reconcile on a fixed cycle, the same day each month, and render the account to the office unprompted. A short monthly summary in the same format every time: spend by category against budget with variances explained, the float or petty-cash reconciliation, any unusual item and its reason, upcoming costs the office should anticipate, and any approval you are requesting.
- A family office forgives a great deal from someone whose numbers are always tidy and always early, and forgives almost nothing from someone whose numbers arrive late and need chasing.

**3.5 · Petty cash**

**Petty cash.** A small float of house money for immediate low-value costs, held in a box or envelope, reconciled to the exact penny on a fixed cycle.

Handle it with the same rigour as large sums, because it is the small, casual, undocumented spending that erodes trust fastest. Every disbursement is logged as it happens. Every receipt goes back into the box in place of the note that left it, so that cash plus receipts always equals the float.

You top up only against a clean reconciliation, never against a vague sense that it is running low.

A petty-cash box that cannot be reconciled to the penny is not a small problem. It is the specific problem that makes a family quietly wonder what else in the house is untidy, and that wondering, once it starts, does not stop at the cash box.

**3.6 · The commission, and why it is fatal**

A supplier will one day offer you a percentage. It will not be presented as a bribe. It will be a "finder's fee", a "trade discount we can share", a case of wine at Christmas that becomes two, a hotel that upgrades you personally.

It is one of the oldest arrangements in this industry and entirely normal in some adjacent trades, which is precisely why it is so easy to accept.

Refuse it, and tell the house the same day. Not because you are pious, but because of what it does to you structurally: the moment you take it you no longer work for the family, you work for the supplier, and every recommendation you make thereafter is compromised.

You will know it, and eventually so will they. In this world it is called a kickback, and there is no recovery from it.

The forms it wears, so you recognise each one:

- The straight cash percentage on invoices you approve.
- The "trade price" a supplier extends to you personally on your own purchases.
- The upgrade, the weekend, the ticket, given to you and not to the family.
- The introduction fee for sending a name into the house.
- The gift from a vendor that grows, quietly, year on year.

Note the tell: a benefit the supplier expects you to keep to yourself is, by that expectation alone, disqualified. The light is the test. Anything that must be hidden is not a thank-you, it is a hook.

**3.7 · When a supplier offers you a genuine discount**

Sometimes the offer is honest: a real trade discount, a lower rate, a value returned. It does not belong to you. It belongs to the household, and your move is to route it there, openly and in writing, and to be visibly pleased to do so.

The script, said warmly and at once: "That's kind, thank you. I can't take anything personally, but the household would be glad of the discount, so please apply it to their account and put it on the invoice." Then note it in your monthly report.

You have lost nothing you were entitled to, and you have shown the office, in the plainest possible way, whose side you are on. A house delights in the person who hands the advantage back.

**3.8 · Gifts, from the principal and from third parties**

Two sources, two entirely different rules. Keep them separate in your mind.

**From the principal.** A principal may press a generous present on you at Christmas or after a hard season, and to refuse the modest and heartfelt is itself a small rudeness. Accept graciously. Thank once, briefly, in person if you can. Then never mention it again. Do not photograph it. Do not wear it in front of them for at least a season. Never speak of its value, and never to another member of staff, because the gift that is discussed becomes a grievance in someone else's hands. A gift accepted with too much emotion changes the relationship as surely as a gift refused.

Where the gift is large, note it privately, mention it once to the office, and let the light fall on it. A gift from the principal that is recorded is a kindness. The recording protects you if anyone ever asks how you came to own it.

**From a third party.** Here the default inverts: you refuse. A gift from a vendor, an agent, a guest, or anyone with an interest in the house is presumed to be a hook until proven otherwise, and the proof is rarely there. The modest, unambiguous token, a card, flowers, a single bottle at Christmas, you may accept and log. Anything beyond that you decline or surrender to the house.

The script for surrender: "How thoughtful, thank you. I'll add it to the house so everyone can enjoy it." The wine goes to the cellar, the hamper to the kitchen, the case to the household. It stops being a private obligation and becomes a shared, recorded, harmless thing, which is exactly what you want.

**3.9 · Tipping culture and staff gratuities**

- When you distribute tips or gratuities on the principal's behalf, on a charter, at a hotel, to visiting crew, do it against the house's standard where one exists, record the amount and the recipient, and never let a tip pass through your hands unlogged. Gratuities are the softest cash in the house and the easiest to be doubted over.
- Tips left for the household staff by guests belong to the staff, distributed by the house's convention, not privately captured by whoever happened to take the envelope. If you are unsure of the convention, ask the office rather than deciding.
- A tip offered to you personally by a guest for ordinary service is usually declined with grace: "That's very kind, but it's my pleasure, please don't." Where declining would cause real awkwardness, in some cultures it genuinely does, accept it and mention it to the house rather than pocketing it silently.
- Never solicit, never hint, never leave the tray in view. The gratuity you angled for is worse than none.

**3.10 · Borrowing, lending, and personal purchases**

Separate your money from theirs, absolutely and permanently.

- Never lend money to the principal, to a colleague, or to a member of staff, and never borrow from any of them. A loan in either direction inside a household is a rope that binds two people who must remain professional, and it always frays on the side of the junior.
- Never buy something for yourself on the house card "and settle up", and never let a personal item ride on a household order to get the trade price. The moment your shopping and theirs share a receipt, you have created the exact ambiguity this chapter exists to prevent.
- If you buy from a supplier the house also uses, buy at the public price, on your own card, on a separate transaction, and keep the two worlds from touching.
- Never hold, mind, or move money for the principal in your own name or your own account. If you are asked to, decline and route it to the office: "That should go through the office so it's properly on the record, I'd rather not hold it personally."

**3.11 · Pricing and invoicing your own extra work**

You will sometimes be asked to do work that sits outside your role: to project-manage a renovation, to source and buy at scale, to run an event. Extra work is legitimately paid for, and the way you handle the money is what keeps it clean.

- Agree the terms before you begin, in writing, however informal. What the work is, what it pays, whether it is a fee or an hourly rate or simply your reimbursed costs, and who approves it. "Happy to take that on. Can we just note the scope and the fee with the office first, so it's clean for both of us?"
- Bill for your time or take a fee, but never take a margin on what you buy. The instant you mark up a purchase, you have re-invented the commission from the other side of the table, and it will read exactly as badly.
- Invoice plainly. An itemised invoice to the office, your costs passed through at cost with receipts attached, your fee shown as a separate line. Nothing bundled, nothing rounded, nothing that requires trust to accept.
- Where the principal offers you a bonus for the extra effort, that is theirs to give and yours to receive, openly and recorded through the office, not a private cash envelope you never mention.

**3.12 · The paper that protects you**

**The record.** Your own dated, factual, unemotional log of money handled, instructions received, and decisions taken. Kept not to accuse anyone, but because one day you will need to remember exactly what was said, and memory is not evidence.

- Where there is a threshold for approval, respect it even when it is inconvenient, and especially when the principal has told you not to bother. Their spoken instruction does not protect you; the office's written record does. Get the approval in a message before you spend, every time.
- When you are told to do something with money that departs from the rules, "pay this early", "don't put this one through", "just handle it in cash", confirm it back in writing before you act: "Just to confirm, you'd like me to settle this directly. Happy to, I'll note it for the office." The confirmation is not distrust. It is the thing that stands between you and a later question you cannot answer.
- Keep the record where you, and only you, control it, and keep it dull. The log that reads like an accusation is a liability; the log that reads like an accountant's is a shield.

**3.13 · The exact words to decline money cleanly**

Learn these by heart, because you will not have time to compose one in the moment, and an improvised refusal comes out either preachy or weak.

- To a supplier offering a personal cut: "That's kind, but I can't take anything personally. If there's a saving in it, put it on the household's invoice and they'll be delighted."
- To a vendor pressing a gift on you: "Thank you, that's thoughtful. I'll add it to the house so everyone can share it."
- To a guest offering you a private tip: "That's very kind, but it's genuinely my pleasure. Please don't."
- To anyone asking you to hold or move their money: "That should really go through the office, so it's on the record. I'd rather not handle it personally."
- To a principal asking you to spend around a rule: "Of course. Let me just confirm it with the office first, so it's clean for everyone."

You do not argue. You do not moralise. You do not explain your principles. Each of these is warm, brief, and closed, and each ends the conversation without leaving a bruise. A line drawn in calm holds; a line you must find in the moment does not.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

Ambiguity about money is indistinguishable from dishonesty, so you eliminate ambiguity: a house card or a float, never your own funds; every receipt captured on the day; petty cash reconciled to the penny; a tidy monthly account rendered early and unprompted. Refuse the supplier commission in every disguise and route every genuine advantage back to the house in writing.@@P@@Accept the principal's modest gift graciously and let the light fall on the large one; presume the third party's gift is a hook and surrender it to the household. Keep tips logged, lending forbidden, and your money and theirs forever separate. Price your extra work honestly, at cost plus a stated fee, never a hidden margin.@@P@@Confirm every departure from the rules in writing before you act, and decline money with words you prepared long before you needed them. It is not a moral question. It is a structural one.

## The politics of a household

*A sealed system with no appeal*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Enter a house as the new person and earn position without provoking the people already there. Hold neutrality in a family or staff conflict while remaining useful. Take instructions that contradict each other from a principal, a spouse and a family office, and survive all three.@@P@@Refuse to carry gossip, correct staff without making enemies, and build the alliances that protect you rather than the ones that end you.

**4.1 · The system you have joined**

Module 1 told you who the players are. This chapter is the code for moving among them. The house is a sealed political system: no human resources, no grievance procedure, no appeal, and decisions made on feeling and made fast.

You can be flawless at the work and gone by spring because you misread the room. Treat the politics as part of the job, not as a distraction from it.

Two facts govern everything that follows. The family will always protect the old over the new, because the old are known and you are not. And nothing you say in this house stays where you said it. Speak and act as though both are true, because both are.

**DEFINITION**

**Standing.** Your informal weight in the house: how far your word is trusted, whose calls you can make alone, who defers to you. It is granted slowly by conduct and withdrawn instantly by a single visible error. You do not ask for standing; you accumulate it.

**4.2 · Being new, and earning position**

Your first ninety days are watched by everyone and remembered longer than you think. The house is not asking whether you are competent; they assumed that when they hired you. They are asking whether you are safe. Answer that question and the rest follows.

- Do the work as it is currently done before you improve anything. Learn the existing method, follow it exactly, and only propose a change once you can name the reason the old way exists. Nothing marks a newcomer as a liability faster than reorganising a system they have not yet understood.
- Say little in the first weeks and observe more than you speak. Map who actually holds power, which is rarely the org chart. Find the person the principal listens to, the person the staff protect, and the person everyone quietly works around.
- Be early, be tidy, and finish what you start visibly. Reputation in the first quarter is built on small completed things, not large promised ones.
- Credit generously and claim nothing. In the early months every good outcome you can attribute to someone already there buys you an ally at no cost to yourself.

**THE FIRST NO**

You will, early on, be tested with a request that is slightly outside the rules: a small favour, a shortcut, a confidence. How you handle the first one sets your price for all the rest. Decline the improper ones warmly and without lecture, keep the promises you make small and then keep them exactly, and let the house learn that your yes is reliable because your no is real.

**4.3 · The long-serving who resists you**

The PA of twelve years. The chauffeur of fifteen. The nanny who raised the children. They cannot be beaten, and they should not be beaten. Where they resist you, understand what the resistance is: not malice, but fear that the newcomer will change the house they have shaped, or expose them, or displace them. Remove the fear and most resistance dissolves.

The method is simple and slightly humbling. Ask their advice, take it visibly, and credit them in front of the principal. They have no ambition to take your role; they have their own, and it is secure. In exchange they will tell you things that would otherwise cost you three years to learn.

Where a long-serving member actively obstructs you, do not escalate to the principal, who will side with the person they have known for a decade. Instead go to them directly and privately, and frame it as needing them rather than correcting them: "You know this house far better than I do.

I need your help getting this right." Make them the author of the solution. A person who feels consulted defends the outcome; a person who feels overruled sabotages it.

If the obstruction continues and genuinely endangers the work, document it factually and calmly, without accusation, and raise it only with whoever manages the staff, framed as an operational problem, never as a complaint about a person. You are describing a broken process, not asking anyone to be judged.

**4.4 · The gatekeepers, and how to treat them**

Every principal at this level is reached through people, and those people decide whether you are reached in return. The private assistant who controls the diary, the family office manager who controls approvals, the head of security, the senior housekeeper who has the principal's ear at the end of the day: these are the gatekeepers. Their formal rank may be below yours. Their real power is not.

- Treat the gatekeeper as a principal in miniature. Return their calls first, answer their questions completely, and never make them chase you. The assistant who has to ask you twice for the same thing will remember it, and their memory reaches the principal.
- Never go around a gatekeeper to reach the person behind them. It is the single fastest way to make a permanent enemy of someone who can close every door you need open. If the assistant controls the diary, you book through the assistant, always, even when you have the principal's mobile number.
- Feed the gatekeeper information before they have to ask for it. The assistant who is never surprised by you will protect you; the one you surprise will manage you out.
- Keep the family office relationship strictly clean and strictly documented. They are the gatekeeper of money and of the record, and their record, not the principal's affection, is what protects you when a question is asked in a year.

**THE ASSISTANT IS YOUR ALLY OR YOUR JUDGE**

The principal's assistant sees everything you send, hears how the principal speaks of you, and is asked, quietly, whether you are working out. Make that person's job easier every single day and they become the most valuable ally in the house. Make it harder even once and you have acquired a judge who sits closer to the principal than you ever will.

**4.5 · Never take a side**

In a staff conflict there is no winning side. There is only the side that leaves, and it is usually the newest person, because the family protects the old. So you do not enter other people's fights, and you do not let yourself be recruited into them.

- Never criticise a colleague to the principal, even when asked directly, and especially then. It is a test, whether or not the principal knows they are setting one. "She is finding her feet, and I am helping her" is a complete answer, and it is usually also true.
- When two colleagues are in open conflict and both come to you, refuse the role of judge and hand it back: "I can see you're both under real pressure. This is something you'll sort out better than I can." Then leave. The moment you rule on it, the loser is your enemy and the winner assumes you are recruitable.
- Do not carry grievances upward. Solve what you can at your level, absorb what you must, and escalate only what genuinely endangers the family or the house.
- Keep your own conduct so clean that you are never the story. In a house without an appeal process, the person with no visible faults is the person who survives the purge.

**THE PHRASING THAT KEEPS YOU OUT WHILE STAYING USEFUL**

You need sentences that decline the fight without declining the work. Learn these:

- "I'd rather not get into who's right, but let me help with the actual problem." Then solve the practical thing and ignore the political one.
- "That's above me, honestly. I'd take it to the office." Said warmly, this closes the subject and points it where it belongs.
- "I only saw part of it, so I couldn't really say." True, modest, and impossible to quote against anyone.
- "You two know each other far better than I do." Handing the conflict back to its owners is not weakness; it is the correct filing of it.

**4.6 · Gossip, and what to do when it is carried to you**

You never carry gossip. Not up, not down, not sideways, not the flattering kind, not the kind you are certain is true. The staff member who trades in information becomes, very quickly, the staff member no one trusts with any, and trust is the whole of your value.

The harder skill is receiving it, because gossip will be carried to you constantly, and often as a gift or a bid for alliance. The rule is to receive it without becoming a link in its chain. Do not react, do not repeat it, do not reward the teller with interest or a second story of your own.

The move is to acknowledge the person while declining the content: "I try not to hold on to that sort of thing, but thank you for trusting me." Warm, closed, and it teaches them not to bring you the next one. If it is a matter of safety or of the family's genuine welfare, that is not gossip; that goes to the office in writing, factually, the same day. Everything else stops with you and dies there.

Never be the one who confirms. Half of gossip travels only because someone reliable nodded. When you are the person who neither denies nor confirms, you make yourself useless to the rumour mill, which is exactly where you want to be.

**4.7 · Correcting staff without making enemies**

You will manage people, and you will need to correct them, and the way you do it decides whether they become loyal or become a quiet campaign against you. The principle is simple: correct the work in private, praise the person in public, and never let a correction be overheard.

- Never reprimand anyone in front of the principal, a guest, or another staff member. A correction with an audience is not a correction; it is a humiliation, and the person will remember the audience long after they have forgotten the fault.
- Speak to the standard, not to the character. "This needs to be done this way, and here's why" is a correction. "You're careless" is an insult. The first is followed; the second is resented and repeated.
- Give the reason. Staff at this level comply far better when they understand the standard than when they are simply ordered to it. A reason turns an instruction into a shared aim.
- Correct once, clearly, then let it go. Do not raise the same fault twice in a week, and never store faults to produce later. The manager who keeps a ledger of grievances is feared, and fear, as this house teaches everywhere, produces sabotage, not improvement.
- Close every correction by restoring the person. "I know you'll have it right next time, and I'm glad you're here" costs a sentence and buys you a subordinate who wants to do well for you.

**4.8 · Protecting a subordinate**

If people report to you, their mistakes are yours in front of the principal, and their protection is your duty. This is not kindness; it is how you earn a team that will not let you fall.

When a subordinate errs, you take the correction upward yourself and you do not name them to the principal unless directly and unavoidably asked. "It was handled on my side and it's already fixed" absorbs the blame at your level, which is where a good manager holds it.

In private, you address it with the person; in public, you own it. A team learns within weeks whether their manager shields them or serves them up, and they repay the answer exactly.

The limit is honesty. You protect a subordinate from unfair blame and from public humiliation; you do not lie to the principal to cover a real fault, and you do not conceal anything that touches safety, money, or the family's welfare. Shielding a person from embarrassment is loyalty; concealing a genuine problem is the improper request wearing a friendly face.

**4.9 · Instructions that conflict**

Sooner or later a principal, a spouse, and a family office will each tell you something that contradicts the others, and you will be standing in the middle holding three instructions and a deadline. You do not choose between them, and you do not quietly decide who is right. You surface the conflict and let its owners resolve it.

- The rule of authority: on the matter in question, follow the person who owns that matter. The office owns money, contracts, and thresholds; the principal owns their own affairs; the spouse owns theirs. When a principal's instruction crosses the office's threshold for approval, the threshold wins, and you say so warmly: "Of course, I'll just clear it with the office so it's on record, then it's done."
- When two instructions genuinely collide and you cannot obey both, do not pick. Go back to the more senior party or to the office, state the conflict plainly and without editorial, and ask them to resolve it: "I've been asked for two different things here and I want to get it right. Which would you like me to follow?"
- Never play the two parties against each other, never carry "well, she said" between them, and never let one believe you defied them when in fact you were following the other. Put your instructions in writing to yourself, dated, so that when you are asked later what you were told, you have the answer and not a memory.
- Put nothing in your own judgement that belongs in theirs. The staff member who resolves a principal-versus-office conflict on their own initiative is the staff member who is blamed by whichever side loses.

**4.10 · Two principals, and the message with an edge**

Where there are two principals, they will not always want the same thing, and one day you will be standing between them holding a message. Serve both. Favour neither.

Carry a message exactly as given: never add the edge it lacks, and never sand off the edge it has. You are not a diplomat, and improvised diplomacy between spouses is precisely how staff are dismissed by the one they were trying to protect.

If you are asked, gently, to keep something from the other, decline at once and warmly, before it hardens into a pattern with no exit: "I'd rather not be in the middle of that, I hope you understand." It costs you a moment of awkwardness.

Its alternative costs you the role. The same applies to a child asking you to conceal something from a parent, or one family member from another: you do not become anyone's secret-keeper against anyone else in the house.

**4.11 · Alliances that are safe, and ones that are not**

You need allies, but the wrong alliance is more dangerous than none. The test is simple: a safe alliance survives being seen by the principal, and an unsafe one depends on not being seen.

The safe ones: the gatekeepers, whom you help daily and expect nothing from beyond a fair hearing; the long-serving, whom you consult and credit; a mentor at another house, with whom you discuss the shape of a problem and never its content; the family office, kept clean and documented. These are relationships you would happily have the principal witness.

The unsafe ones: any pairing built on a shared secret, a shared complaint, or a shared enemy inside the house. The colleague who wants to grumble with you about the principal is not offering friendship; they are recruiting a witness and a co-defendant. Faction alliances, where the staff split into camps, are the fastest route out, because when the family tires of the friction they remove whole camps at once, and the newest member of a camp goes first.

Decline the camp warmly, stay on decent terms with everyone, and belong to no one but the house.

**4.12 · The single point of failure**

It is tempting to make yourself irreplaceable by holding everything in your own head: the passwords, the contacts, the arrangements, the file only you can read. It feels like security. It is the opposite.

Families do not reward staff who cannot be replaced; they fear them, and fear does not produce promotion. It produces a quiet, deliberate reduction of your access, and eventually a replacement recruited in secret. The professionals who last are those who document everything so completely that they could be replaced tomorrow, and who are, for exactly that reason, never replaced. Your standing comes from being trusted, not from being a hostage.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

The household is a political system without an appeal, and the family protects the old over the new. Earn position slowly: learn the existing method, credit others, make your no reliable. Turn the long-serving into allies by consulting and crediting them; treat the gatekeepers, whatever their rank, as people who can open or close every door.@@P@@Take no side, carry no gossip and let none pass through you, and correct staff privately while protecting subordinates publicly. When instructions conflict, surface the conflict and let its owners resolve it; carry no edged message between two principals and keep no secret between them.@@P@@Build only the alliances that survive being seen, and document everything, because irreplaceability is a weakness disguised as power.

## The improper request

*The one that ends careers, and the exact words that do not*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Grade a request from grey to plainly criminal before you have agreed to anything. Separate the distasteful, which you may swallow, from the improper, which you deflect, from the criminal, which you refuse absolutely. Say no to a principal without wounding the relationship.@@P@@Know when to put nothing in writing and when to insist on it, how to protect yourself if you are pressured, and how to leave if wrongdoing becomes the condition of the job.

**5.1 · Three words that are not the same**

Most people collapse everything unwelcome into a single feeling of discomfort and then act on the feeling. That is the error. Discomfort is not information; the category is. Before you respond to anything that troubles you, sort it into one of three, because each has a different protocol and confusing them is how good people either overreact or comply.

**Distasteful.** Lawful, harmless to others, but beneath you or tedious or faintly demeaning. Walking the dog of the principal's guest. Being spoken to sharply. Waiting three hours in a car. This is not an improper request at all. It is the job, and the professional swallows it without a flicker.

**Improper.** It deceives, exposes, or uses your position for an end that is not the household's. Not necessarily illegal. Confirming to a caller when the house is empty. Telling one spouse what the other spent. Passing a name to a supplier for a fee. This is the grey country, and it is where careers quietly erode, one small favour at a time.

**Criminal.** It breaks the law, or would make you a party to someone else breaking it. Falsifying a document. Moving money to obscure its origin. Lying to a police officer or a court. Backdating a contract. Here there is no grading and no negotiation. You do not do it, whatever it costs, because the cost of doing it is always higher.

The discipline is to name the category first, silently, before you speak. The moment you have named it, you know your script.

**5.2 · The grades, grey to black**

Within the improper and the criminal there is a ladder, and you should be able to place a request on it in the first few seconds, because your handling changes with the rung.

- **Grey, and probably innocent.** A thing that could be normal or could be the first step of something. "How long are they away in August?" from a friend. You deflect, blandly, and let it go. No drama.
- **Grey, and using you.** A pattern beginning. The guest's errand that becomes the guest's business that becomes the household card paying for it. You decline the small thing early, while declining is still easy, and you notice the direction of travel.
- **Improper and clear.** Deceiving a spouse, hiding a purchase, saying you were somewhere you were not. You decline warmly and you do not become the mechanism.
- **Criminal.** Falsification, money movement, lying to an authority. You refuse plainly, you put your refusal on record, and if it is pressed you prepare to leave.

The reason to grade fast is that most improper requests are made in a heat that passes. Grade it low and you can often let time do the work. Grade it high and you must act with your whole spine, immediately, because a criminal request that is entertained for an afternoon is one you are already half inside.

**5.3 · The shape it takes**

It comes for everyone, usually within the first year, and never in the form you rehearsed. It will be small. It will be reasonable. It will be delivered with a smile by someone charming, and it will be very easy to say yes.

A journalist who is "only confirming something we already have". A friend of the family, met at the house a dozen times, who asks warmly how long it will be empty in August. A supplier who would be so grateful for an introduction.

The assistant of someone important, who needs "just the address, we have it anyway". A member of the family, usually not the principal, who asks you to keep something from the other. An instruction to alter a date on a document, or to say you were somewhere you were not. It will be trivial. It will be the beginning.

**5.4 · Why the charming version is the dangerous one**

Note the technique in the journalist's line: the caller claims to know already, so that confirming feels like nothing. Note the friend's: familiarity dissolves judgment, which is exactly why a real breach almost always arrives wearing the face of a friend rather than the face of a stranger.

The principal's version is more dangerous still, because to it is added authority and your own loyalty. The improper request from the person you serve does not feel improper. It feels like being trusted.

That feeling is the whole of the trap, and the only defence against it is to have decided, in the calm of today, what you will not do, so that you are not deciding it in the warmth of the moment.

**5.5 · Saying no to a principal without losing the role**

This is the skill the profession is really testing, and it is a technique, not a temperament. Refusing a principal badly costs you the role as surely as complying does. There is a way to decline that leaves their dignity and yours intact, and it has four moves.

First, you never refuse the person; you decline the action, and you decline it as though the difficulty were external and practical rather than moral. You do not say "I won't lie for you." You say "I can't put a false date on that, it would sit on the record and I'd hate for it to come back on you." The refusal is dressed as protection of them, which is what it usually genuinely is.

Second, you carry an alternative in the same breath. A bare no leaves a vacuum, and a principal in a heat fills a vacuum with anger. "I can't send that message as it stands, but let me draft you a version that says the same thing and can't be used against you" gives them the substance of what they wanted and removes the part that would harm them. Most improper requests have a proper core; find it and offer it.

Third, you buy time, because most heat passes. "Let me look into that properly and come back to you within the hour" is very often the entire solution. Within the hour the impulse has cooled, the meeting that caused it is further away, and the request has quietly withdrawn itself. You were never asked to refuse; you were asked to wait, and waiting refused it for you.

Fourth, you never moralise, never argue, never let a flicker of judgment cross your face. The principal must not feel caught or corrected. You are simply the person for whom this particular thing is, regrettably, not possible, and who has already found them the thing that is.

**A PRINCIPAL WHO HAS WATCHED YOU DECLINE**

There is a hidden dividend in all of this. A principal who has watched you quietly decline to do the wrong thing on their behalf has learned the single most valuable fact about you: that you will not do it to them either. The clean refusal, handled without theatre, is not a mark against you. Over years it is the foundation of the trust that keeps you.

**5.6 · The grey request: delay and deflect**

For the grey and probably innocent, and for the grey that is beginning to use you, confrontation is the wrong tool. It is disproportionate, it makes you seem precious, and it converts an ambiguous moment into a standoff you may lose. The instrument is deflection: a bland, closed, unmemorable answer that gives nothing and accuses no one.

- To "how long are they away?": "I honestly don't keep track of their plans, the office would know." Warm, unremarkable, and finished.
- To the errand that is drifting into someone's private business: "That's a bit outside what I can pick up, I'm afraid, but I'll pass it to the office." You have declined the thing without declining the person.
- To "just this once, on the house card": "I can't run that one through the household account, but happy to point you to how to sort it directly." No lecture. A door closed softly.

Deflection buys the same thing delay buys: it lets an innocent request evaporate and forces a serious one to be made again, more plainly, at which point it is no longer grey and you handle it as what it has become.

**5.7 · The hard lines**

Some things are never graded, never delayed, never softened with an alternative. You refuse them outright, and you should know them by name now, in the cold, so that you recognise them instantly in the warm. You never agree to:

- **Anything illegal.** Falsifying, backdating, or altering a document. Lying to a court, a police officer, a tax authority, an insurer, or a border. Destroying anything that may be evidence. There is no version of this that your loyalty makes acceptable.
- **Moving money to disguise it.** Carrying cash across a border. Structuring payments to sit under a threshold. Routing a sum through your own account "to keep it simple". Signing for funds whose purpose you cannot see. Money that wants to move quietly is the single most dangerous thing you will ever be asked to touch.
- **Lying to a spouse in a way that carries real risk.** Covering an affair is a country you must not enter, and the reason is practical as much as moral: you become the only witness to a deception, and when the marriage breaks, and one day it may, the witness is the person who is removed, generously and without explanation. You do not hold that secret. You decline to be placed in the middle of it, early, before it is a pattern.
- **Deceiving an authority on the family's behalf.** Telling the police the principal was home. Confirming to an official a fact you know to be false. The moment you speak the untruth you have made their problem your crime.

For these there is no clever alternative and no time to buy. There is only the plain refusal, and then the record.

**5.8 · Writing: nothing, or everything**

People assume the rule is always to avoid a paper trail. It is not. The rule has two halves, and knowing which half you are in is itself a skill.

You put nothing in writing when writing would create the very record the improper request wants. Never confirm a movement, an address, an empty house, or a private fact in a message, even to decline elaborately, because the thread is evidence and your careful denial still confirms that you were asked and that you knew.

To the press and to the fishing caller you say your line aloud, briefly, and you do not type it.

You put everything in writing the moment a request has troubled you enough to refuse it. This is the reversal that protects you. The same day, in one factual paragraph to the office or to whoever stands above the person who asked: who asked, when, what they wanted, what you said.

No drama, no accusation, no guessing at their motive. If it was innocent, nothing happens and you have lost nothing. If it was not, you are the person who noticed, and a household cannot afford to lose the person who notices.

And keep your own quiet note as well, dated and unemotional, of what you were asked and how you responded. Not to wield against anyone, but because one day you may need to remember exactly what was said, and memory is not evidence. Trust and a private record are not opposites; the record is what lets you go on being trusted.

**5.9 · If you are pressured**

Sometimes the request does not withdraw. It is repeated, more firmly, with warmth removed, and you feel the temperature of the room change. This is the moment the profession is really about, and there are a few fixed rules for it.

Do not argue the ethics. You will not win a moral debate with someone who has already decided, and winning it would cost you the role anyway. Stay on the practical register: it can't be done, here is what can, let me sort that for you now.

Do not do it "just once to keep the peace". There is no once. The first compliance is a fact about you that the household now owns, and it will be asked for again, with the first time as the argument.

Slow everything down. "I want to get this right for you, let me take an hour." Pressure relies on speed. Almost nothing that is genuinely urgent is also genuinely improper; the combination is the tell.

Put your refusal on the record the same day, factually, to the office. Documentation around the very things this chapter warns of is your protection if the matter ever surfaces, and it very occasionally does.

And do not threaten, hint, or make yourself dramatic. You are calm, you are regretful, you are immovable. The immovability is quiet.

**5.10 · When it becomes the condition of the job**

Rarely, the wrongdoing is not a passing heat but a standing expectation. The role, you come to understand, requires you to lie routinely, to hold a criminal secret, to be the mechanism of something you cannot be part of. When that is true, the calculation is already made, and it was made before you arrived.

You leave. You leave well, in the manner the profession requires: you serve your notice if you safely can, you hand over cleanly, and you say nothing to anyone, then or later. You do not denounce, you do not threaten to expose, you do not negotiate a price for your silence, which is itself a crime.

If what you have been asked to do or conceal is serious enough, you take proper advice, quietly, from a lawyer, not from a colleague.

This is exactly why Module 1 insisted on a life and a self outside the role. The person who has poured everything into the family, who has no independence and no self beyond it, is the person who cannot say no, cannot risk the relationship, and cannot walk away from the compromise, because to lose the role would be to lose everything.

The professional who can leave is the only one who can truly refuse, and being able to refuse is, in the end, what you are being paid for.

**5.11 · The prepared refusals**

**LEARN THESE BY HEART**

To the press: "I'm not able to help with that." Then end the call, courteously, and add nothing. Do not confirm. Do not deny, because a denial is information. Do not say "I'll have to check", which confirms that you could.

To the charming friend: "I honestly don't keep track of the family's plans, the office would know." Warm, unremarkable, and closed.

To the supplier seeking an introduction or offering a fee: "I don't make introductions, I'm afraid, but do send your details to the office." Nothing about the fee. You did not hear it.

To the principal, on the document: "I can't put a false date on that, it would sit on the record and come back on you, but let me sort the proper version now." Practical, protective, and paired with a way forward.

To the spouse asking you to conceal: "I'd rather not be in the middle of that, I hope you understand." Warm, immediate, and final, before it becomes a pattern from which there is no exit.

To anything that troubles you and does not fit a script: "I'm not able to help with that, but let me pass it to the office." You do not argue. You do not moralise. You do not improvise. A line drawn in calm holds; a line you must find in the moment does not.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

Name the category before you speak: distasteful is swallowed, improper is deflected, criminal is refused absolutely. Grade fast, because most improper requests are made in a heat that passes, and time, an hour, a bland answer, will often refuse them for you. Say no to a principal by declining the action, not the person, dressing it as their protection, and carrying an alternative in the same breath.@@P@@Never move money quietly, never falsify, never lie to an authority, never hold the secret of an affair. Put nothing in writing that the request wants recorded, and put everything in writing the moment you have had to refuse. Keep a self outside the role, because only the person who can leave can truly say no.

## Boundaries, and the cost of this work

*The code for keeping a self, a life, and a limit inside a role with no natural edges*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Hold warmth and familiarity apart, and know the exact behaviours that keep the line. Protect real time off inside an "always on" culture, using specific language and structure. Recognise the wrong kind of indispensability, the confidante drift, and the private appetites that end careers.@@P@@Refuse scope creep without friction, and leave the role at the door each day. Treat burnout as a predictable occupational hazard with a maintenance routine, not a moral failing.

**6.1 · Warmth is the manner, familiarity is the mistake**

Two words that sound alike and are opposites. Learn the difference in your body, because you will make the decision fifty times a day without time to think.

**Warmth.** Attentive, easy, kind, genuinely pleased to be of use. It flows toward the principal and asks nothing back.

**Familiarity.** Warmth that has started to expect reciprocity. It wants to be liked, thanked, confided in, treated as an equal. It flows toward the principal and quietly waits for something to flow back.

The line between them is not about how much you feel. You may feel a great deal. The line is about what you do with it. Warmth serves. Familiarity leans. Hold the warmth and refuse the lean.

Concrete tells that you have crossed into familiarity:

- You offer opinions on the family's decisions before they are requested.
- You use the principal's first name when the house convention is title or surname, because in your head you have been promoted.
- You linger in a room after the work is done, hoping the conversation continues.
- You make jokes that assume shared history, and you feel a small sting when they do not land.
- You start sentences with "We should" about matters that are theirs, not yours.

The correction is small and undramatic. Do the warm thing, then leave the room. Presence that does not overstay is the whole signature of a professional. The moment your usefulness is complete, your reason to remain is complete too.

**6.2 · "Always on" is a culture, not a contract**

The role has no natural edge. Nothing in the day announces that you are finished, because the household never finishes. If you wait for permission to stop, it will not come, and you will simply work until you break. So you build the edge yourself, in advance, in writing, and you defend it calmly.

Structural rules, non-negotiable:

- Agree your genuine off hours before you start, and get them in the contract, not the conversation. "One full day and two evenings a week, phone off from ten" is a term. "We'll see how it goes" is a trap.
- Distinguish an emergency from an inconvenience, out loud, on day one. A pipe has burst is an emergency. The principal cannot find the good corkscrew at eleven at night is not. If you answer the second, you have taught them there is no difference.
- Have a second person. A number the family can reach when you are genuinely off, a colleague, an agency line, a covering butler. A boundary with no backup is a boundary you will breach the first time it is tested.
- Silence the phone on your day off and mean it. Not "on silent, but I'll glance". Off. The one time you glance is the time the culture wins.

When the off-hours call comes, and it will, your tone does the work. Warm, unbothered, brief.

"Of course, let me help you sort that. Give me two minutes." Then, when it is done: "Glad that's settled.

I'm back in properly at eight tomorrow, and I'll pick up everything then." You have helped, and you have restated the edge in the same breath, without a flicker of resentment. Resentment is what happens to people who never drew the line and blame the family for standing on it.

**6.3 · Physical and emotional boundaries with the principal and family**

You will be closer to these people than most of their friends, and further from them than any of their staff imagine. Both distances are correct at once.

Physical rules that read as competence, not coldness:

- Knock, and wait for the reply, on every closed door, every time, including when you are certain the room is empty. The habit protects you on the one day it is not.
- Handle the principal's body only with explicit, functional reason, dressing, medical, mobility, and narrate what you are doing as you do it. "I'm going to take your left arm now." Never touch to comfort unless comfort has been asked for.
- Keep a consistent physical distance in conversation and hold it whether the principal is charming or furious. The distance is the message: I am steady, and the same, in every weather.

Emotional rules:

- You may be told secrets. You are a container, not a participant. Receive, hold, and never trade the secret back for closeness by offering one of your own.
- Do not take sides in the family's conflicts, even when invited, even when one side is plainly right. "That sounds very difficult" is a complete answer. The moment you ally, you become a piece on the board, and pieces get removed.
- Sympathy, yes. Merged feeling, no. When the family grieves you are steady so that they can fall apart safely. Your composure is the service. Save your own weather for your own people, off the property.

**6.4 · The wrong kind of indispensable**

There is a right indispensability and a wrong one, and ambitious people reliably chase the wrong one because it feels like security. It is the opposite.

**Right.** You are indispensable because the house runs beautifully, the systems are documented, and anyone stepping in would find everything legible. You are trusted because you make yourself replaceable and the machine still hums.

**Wrong.** You are indispensable because only you know the codes, the contacts, the passwords, the where-things-are, the how-she-likes-it. You have made yourself the single point of failure, and you feel powerful. You are not powerful. You are a risk the family will eventually decide to retire.

The wrong version corrupts you quietly. You start withholding small pieces of knowledge, keeping the black book in your head rather than the file, being vague in the handover, because your usefulness has become your leverage and you are frightened to let it go. This is a slow professional suicide. The households that keep people for twenty years keep the ones who document everything and hoard nothing.

The test: if you were struck down tonight, could a competent stranger run this house from your files by Friday? If yes, you are safe and valued. If no, you have confused being needed with being secure, and you have built your own trap.

**6.5 · Romance and drink, the two that end it fastest**

Nowhere is the code shorter or harder than here, because these are the two failures that no reference survives.

On romance and attraction:

- No romantic or sexual involvement with the principal, the family, or their inner circle. Not "not while it's complicated". None. The power difference makes real consent a fiction and makes you disposable the instant it cools.
- Attraction is not the failure; acting on it, or letting it colour the work, is. If you notice it, name it privately, add distance, and if the distance will not hold, ask your agency or mentor to move you. Leaving early and clean beats being removed.
- Relationships with fellow staff are a house matter, not a private one. Some houses tolerate them, most do not, and a concealed one discovered is worse than a declared one refused. Know the house rule before, not after.

On drink and its cousins:

- You do not drink on duty. Not a glass while serving, not "just one" at the family party you are staffing. You are the sober adult in every room, always, and that is not a punishment, it is the job.
- When the principal presses a drink on you, and they will, to be generous or to blur the line, decline warmly and without a speech. "That's very kind, I'll have one on my own time. Water's perfect for now." Repeated, calm, unembarrassed.
- Watch your own consumption off duty with more honesty than most professions require, because this work is isolating, well paid, and stressful, which is precisely the chemistry that grows a quiet dependence. If the drink has become the thing that gets you through the week, the week is the problem, and the drink is hiding it.

**6.6 · Protecting your identity and your relationships outside the role**

The role is designed, structurally, to eat everything else. It pays well enough, absorbs enough hours, and flatters you enough that you can lose your outside life without noticing until it is gone. You prevent this deliberately or not at all.

- Keep at least one relationship that has nothing to do with this world and knows nothing about it. Someone who asks how you are, not how the principal is. Guard this person; they are the last mirror that still shows you your own face.
- Never tell your outside people what you should not. Not the names, not the secrets, not the entertaining story. Discretion off the property is the same duty as discretion on it, and the story that gets a laugh at dinner is the story that ends a career. Your outside life is for being yourself, not for spending the family's privacy.
- Have a professional confidant as well, a mentor or a peer at another house, with whom you can discuss the shape of a problem without ever its content. "I've a boundary issue with a principal who keeps calling on my day off" is safe. Names and details are not. This is the pressure valve that keeps people sane for decades.
- Keep one thing that is only yours and predates the job. A sport, a craft, a faith, a Sunday habit. When the role tries to become your whole identity, this is the piece of you it cannot touch.

Money is not a life, and this profession pays well enough that you may not notice you have traded one for the other until several years have quietly passed.

**6.7 · Scope creep, and the art of the easy no**

The job will grow. Not by decision, by drift. A favour becomes a duty, a duty becomes an expectation, and one morning you are doing four roles for one salary and cannot recall agreeing to any of it. You do not stop this with a confrontation. You stop it with a hundred small, calm redirections.

The technique is to say no to the task while saying yes to the person.

- "I'd love to help with that. To do it properly I'd need to hand off the school run, shall I arrange that?" You have not refused. You have made the true cost visible and put the decision back where it belongs.
- "That's really outside what we agreed, but I can find you the right person for it by tomorrow." You solve the problem without absorbing it.
- "Happy to cover this once. If it's going to be regular, let's talk about the role properly." One-off help stays generous; a permanent expansion gets named as one.

Say the easy no early and often, when the stakes are a single small task. People who never say the small no end up needing the large one, and the large one always sounds like a complaint. A boundary defended at task one is a preference. The same boundary defended at task fifty is a grievance.

**6.8 · Staff or person, and how the good houses differ**

You will be treated, on any given day, somewhere on a line between valued professional and invisible furniture. The house's manner tells you almost everything about how long you should intend to stay.

- In a good house you are staff and a person: thanked, named, remembered, paid on time, spoken to as an adult. You give such a house your loyalty and your years.
- In a poor house you are staff only: talked over, tested, blamed downward, treated as a function with a uniform. You may still serve it impeccably, but you serve it with your exit already quietly planned.

Your own conduct does not change with the treatment. You are courteous, excellent, and composed whether you are seen or not, because your standard is yours, not a reward you dispense for good behaviour. But you read the treatment clearly, without bitterness, as data.

Being treated as furniture is not a reason to become resentful. It is a reason to update your plan and keep your reference intact on the way out.

Never argue for your own dignity in the moment. It cannot be won that way, and the attempt costs you the composure that is your only real authority. You demonstrate your worth by the quality of the work and, when the house will not see it, you take that worth to a house that will.

**6.9 · Burnout is an occupational hazard, so treat it like one**

Burnout in this profession does not look like collapse until the very end. For most of its life it looks like dedication. That is what makes it dangerous, and that is why you manage it as a known risk, structurally, before you feel it.

The early symptoms, learn them as a checklist:

- You stop taking your days off, and you tell yourself it is because they need you. It is not; it is because you have begun to need being needed.
- You feel a small, private pleasure at being called at midnight.
- You defend the family to your own friends, with heat.
- Small requests produce a flash of anger out of all proportion.
- You cannot remember the last conversation you had that was not about work.

The maintenance habits that prevent it:

- Take every day off, physically off the property. A day off spent in the house is a day of quiet duty wearing a day off's clothes.
- Sleep is a work tool, not a luxury; guard it as you would guard the principal's schedule.
- Move your body daily and eat like an adult, because the job will feed you late, rich, and irregularly if you let it set the terms.
- Keep the professional confidant and use them before the crisis, not during it. A boundary problem discussed at week three is a conversation; discussed at month nine it is a resignation.
- Book real leave in advance and take it. The house that "cannot spare you" for a week is the house that has quietly made you the single point of failure, which is section 6.4 arriving to collect.

Burnout is not weakness and it is not a verdict on your character. It is what happens to a competent person in a role with no natural edges who did not build the edges themselves. You build them, or the job builds a breakdown for you.

**6.10 · Leaving the role at the door, daily and finally**

There are two departures. The small one you perform every day, and the large one you perform once, and the same discipline governs both.

The daily leaving:

- Fix a ritual that marks the seam between the role and yourself. Change out of the uniform, walk a particular route home, put the work phone in a drawer. The body needs a signal that the performance is over, or it never quite is.
- Do not carry the day's residue into your own door. The principal's mood is not your mood. Practise setting it down, deliberately, at the same threshold each night, until it becomes automatic.
- Refuse to let the role narrate your inner life. You are a person who does this work superbly. You are not the work.

The final leaving, when the day comes, and it will:

- Serve your notice in full and hand over completely. The file, the systems, the calendar, the relevant contacts, all of it, generously and without withholding. The instinct to hold a little back as leverage is the wrong indispensability making its last appeal; refuse it.
- Say nothing to anyone, then or later. The discretion does not expire with the contract. The former staff member who talks is finished, quietly and permanently.
- Ask, at the end, for a written reference, and ask warmly and directly. The house you leave impeccably will recommend you for the rest of your working life.

That last point is not sentiment. The exit is the reference, and the reference is the entire mechanism of this industry, described in a single line. Every boundary in this chapter, every calm no and unglamorous day off, exists so that you arrive at that door intact, respected, and free to walk through it into the next chapter of a long career rather than out of a short one.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

Warmth flows out and asks nothing; familiarity leans and waits. Build your own edges into an edgeless role, in writing, and defend them without resentment. Make yourself the right kind of indispensable, the documented kind, never the hoarded kind.@@P@@No romance, no drink on duty, no exceptions. Keep an outside life and one professional confidant, and protect both. Say the small no early so you never need the large one.@@P@@Treat burnout as a hazard with a routine, leave the role at the door each night, and leave the house impeccably at the end, because the exit is the reference, and the reference is the career.

## Case law

*The whole module, reduced to the moment of decision*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Read a situation and name the rule that governs it before you feel the pull to improvise. Each precedent below is a real shape you will meet. Study the ruling, not the story: the story changes every time, the ruling does not. When you can predict the ruling before you reach it, the module has done its work.

**7.1 · The confidence that is fished for**

At a lunch a guest you have served many times leans in, warm and conspiratorial, and says she has heard the principal is selling the London house, is that right. She is not a journalist. She is charming, she already seems to know, and a nod would cost you nothing you can see.

**The ruling.** You say, lightly, that you would not know, the office handles all of that, and you refill her glass. Notice the technique: she claims to know already, so that a nod feels like agreeing rather than revealing. A person who already knew would not be asking you; the question is the tell. Confirmation is information, and you never supply it to a room, however friendly the face across the table.

**7.2 · The percentage that is offered quietly**

A florist you use weekly takes you aside and says that for the volume you send him, he would be glad to return five per cent to you personally, cash, nobody the wiser, and the flowers stay exactly as good. The arrangement is normal in his trade and he presents it as a courtesy between professionals.

**The ruling.** You decline in the moment, keep using him only if he remains the right supplier on the merits, and you write to the office the same day describing what was offered. It will not arrive labelled a bribe; it comes as a finder's fee, a courtesy, a discount you two can share, which is precisely why it is easy to take. The instant you accept his money you work for him, and every recommendation you make afterward is bought. Refuse, disclose, and let the record show you were the one who reported it. Any genuine trade discount, by contrast, belongs to the household, and you say so in writing.

**7.3 · The grey favour that is almost reasonable**

The principal's assistant asks you to back-date a delivery note by two days so an invoice falls into the previous quarter. It is a small thing, it is not your money, and it is not, on its face, your business. She frames it as tidying up a clerical slip.

**The ruling.** You do not alter the document, and you do not argue about accounting, which is not your ground and not the point. You say, without heat, that you are not able to change a dated record but you will happily pass it to the office to sort out. Altering a date is falsifying a record; the size of the lie is irrelevant, and the person who asks a junior to do it is placing the risk on you, not on herself. If it was innocent, nothing is lost by routing it upward; if it was not, you are the one who declined to touch it.

**7.4 · The spouse who wants a secret kept**

One principal draws you aside and asks you, kindly, not to mention to the other that a particular sum was spent, or a particular visitor came. It is said gently, as a small kindness between the two of you, and refusing feels cold and disloyal.

**The ruling.** You decline at once, warmly, before it becomes a habit from which there is no exit: you would rather not be in the middle of that, and you hope they understand. You serve both principals and favour neither. The moment you hold one spouse's secret from the other you have chosen a side, and you will be dismissed by the very person you thought you were protecting.

**7.5 · The gift that is too large**

After a difficult season handled well, a principal presses an expensive watch on you, or an envelope of cash far beyond any ordinary thanks. It is offered with real affection and to refuse it outright would wound them and look ungracious.

**The ruling.** You thank them once, briefly and sincerely, and then you disclose it quietly to the office or the family's manager, because a gift of real value should live on the record rather than in your pocket as a private understanding. You do not photograph it, you do not wear it in front of them for a season, and you never discuss its value with another member of staff, in whose hands it becomes a grievance. Ordinary gifts you accept with grace and never mention again; a gift large enough to look like leverage is one you surface, so that no one can ever say it bought you.

**7.6 · The colleague's small theft**

You notice the chef is padding the grocery float, a little each week, nothing dramatic, and he is otherwise kind to you and has been in the house for years. Saying nothing feels like loyalty. Saying something feels like betrayal of a friend and a risk to yourself.

**The ruling.** You do not confront him, gossip about it, or investigate; you report the fact, dated and factual, without accusation or theory of motive, to the office, and you let them handle it. This is not disloyalty and it is not your judgement to soften; the household, not you, decides what it is and what to do. Silence makes you a participant, and when the pattern is eventually found, and it always is, the question becomes who else knew. Protecting a colleague's theft costs you your own name.

**7.7 · The secret overheard by accident**

Passing a doorway you hear, unmistakably, that the principal has received a diagnosis, or that the company is about to announce something that has not been announced. No one meant you to hear it. You now hold something that could move markets or wound a family.

**The ruling.** You behave, from that second, as though you never heard it: no hint, no changed manner, no mention to a single soul, including the colleague you trust most. Information you were never given is the most dangerous kind, precisely because no one is watching to see whether you keep it. The overheard secret is kept exactly as strictly as the entrusted one.

**7.8 · The request that quietly grows your job**

A weekend task becomes a habit; soon you are managing the principal's brother's flat, then his car, then his own small errands, none of it discussed, none of it agreed, all of it now assumed. You are competent, so it keeps landing on you, and declining now feels like refusing to be helpful.

**The ruling.** You do not simply absorb it and you do not refuse it flatly; you surface it, calmly, to whoever holds your remit, and ask for the new scope to be confirmed, in writing, so expectations are shared. Uncontrolled scope creep ends in a role no one agreed to and a failure that is blamed on you. Naming the boundary early is not laziness; it is how the work stays defined.

**7.9 · The boundary that is being tested**

Late one evening a principal, having drunk a little, becomes over-familiar, keeps you talking long past your hours, and floats an invitation to stay and have a drink, treating you as a friend rather than staff. It is flattering, it is warm, and it is a line moving in real time.

**The ruling.** You stay perfectly courteous, you do not stiffen or lecture, and you make a graceful exit: you are so glad the evening went well, and you will see them in the morning. Then you go. Being trusted feels like being chosen, but it is a professional condition, not a friendship, and the flattery is exactly what dissolves the judgement you were hired to keep. Warmth without intimacy is the whole art; the trusted staff member who becomes a companion becomes a witness, and the witness is always, eventually, moved on.

**7.10 · The mistake you would rather bury**

You realise you have booked the family onto the wrong day of travel, and the error is entirely yours. You believe that with a few frantic hours you can fix it before anyone notices, and telling the office now means owning a failure that might otherwise disappear.

**The ruling.** You report it immediately, in writing, plainly: what happened, its effect, and the two options you have already lined up to remedy it. Owning the error in the same breath as the fix is what separates a professional from a liability. A bad fact delivered early is a problem the house can solve; the same fact delivered late is a crisis about you, and the house will remember the concealment long after it has forgotten the booking. No surprises, ever, even when you are almost certain you can save it quietly.

**7.11 · The camera at the gate**

Leaving a restaurant with the principal you notice a photographer across the street. In the scramble to the car the principal freezes, and a member of the public with a phone begins filming you both, and someone asks you, directly, to confirm who the family is.

**The ruling.** You say nothing, you do not react to the lens, and you move calmly to your role, which is the door of the car, not the argument on the pavement. You never confirm, deny, or engage the press or a bystander with a phone; a denial is information and a reaction is a photograph, and either one becomes the caption. Your only job in that moment is the principal's composure and the shortest clean line to the car. Afterward you report the incident to the office so security is aware, and you let them, not you, decide what if anything is said.

**7.12 · The proud post**

You photograph the table you laid beautifully in the chalet, empty, no faces, just candlelight and the mountains through the window, and you post it because you are proud of your work and it names no one. Days later a journalist places the chalet from that same window, and a stay the family had kept quiet is in print.

**The ruling.** There is no safe photograph from inside the private world, and the rule is total: nothing from any residence, car, aircraft or yacht reaches any account of yours, ever, not for your own mother. A picture need not contain a person to reveal one; the window did it. The post that ends a career is almost never malicious. It is proud.

**7.13 · The account that names your employer**

A former colleague adds you on a public network, and you realise your own profile, taken together with a location tag and a comment or two, would let anyone with patience deduce which family you serve. You have posted nothing secret. You have simply lived online as an ordinary person.

**The ruling.** You strip it back so that no employer can be deduced, remove locations and the tags that place you, and assume the family's security team, a consultant, and occasionally a journalist all look. A single named town beside a single dated photograph is enough for a patient stranger to assemble the rest. In most serious houses a deducible public presence is not a matter of taste but a term of employment. Discretion is a system you run on quiet days, not a reaction you produce on loud ones.

**7.14 · The friend who asks when the house is empty**

At a party an old friend, entirely without malice, asks what your summer looks like, and it would be the most natural thing in the world to say that you finally get three weeks off in August because the family will all be away. It is small talk. It is a friendly room.

**The ruling.** You keep it vague: you are hoping for some time off, nothing is settled, and you turn the conversation. When a residence stands empty is security information, and it does not become harmless because the person asking means no harm. The room being friendly is exactly the condition under which the guard drops, which is why the rule holds hardest there.

**7.15 · The supplier who wants an introduction**

A contractor who has done genuinely good work, and been generous and kind to you personally, asks only for a warm introduction to another family you know, or to the principal directly, so he can grow his business. It feels ungrateful to refuse a decent man a small favour.

**The ruling.** You do not make the introduction and you do not improvise a reason; you say simply that you do not make introductions, but he is welcome to send his details to the office. Your access to other households is not yours to trade, and a favour done from gratitude is still a door opened without permission. Kindness received does not create an obligation you are not entitled to pay.

**7.16 · The reference for a friend leaving badly**

A colleague you like is being let go and asks you, before they go, to slip them a copy of the household contact list, or the principal's private numbers, so they land on their feet elsewhere. They are hurt, they feel wronged, and you feel for them.

**The ruling.** You refuse, gently and without a lecture, because the black book and the contacts belong to the house, not to whoever happens to hold them. You may help a friend with warmth, a kind word, an honest personal reference from your own name, but never with the household's information. Sympathy is not a licence to remove what was never yours to give.

**7.17 · The instruction to place you where you were not**

The principal, in a rush, asks you to tell someone, a lawyer, a spouse, an official, that they were somewhere they were not, or that a call happened that did not. It is framed as trivial, a small social cover, and it is the principal themselves who asks, which makes refusal feel close to insubordination.

**The ruling.** You do not lie on anyone's behalf, and you decline without drama: you would rather not say that, but you are glad to say nothing at all. An instruction from the principal does not protect you from the consequence of the lie; you are the one who spoke it, and you are the one it later belongs to, especially if lawyers or an official ever ask. Note that this refusal is the same shape as declining to alter a date or to keep a secret between spouses: a small falsehood offered by someone with authority over you, which is the exact form the improper request always takes. Loyalty is doing the work impeccably, not carrying a falsehood that will one day have your name on it.

## Glossary of the module

**Information hygiene.** The systematic management of what is recorded, said, sent and kept about a principal. Movement information, Where the family is, when, and when a residence is empty. Always treated as security information. Kickback, A commission or benefit from a supplier. Fatal, and structurally so. The improper request, A request that should not be fulfilled, as distinct from one that cannot be. The confidante trap, The drift from trusted professional to personal confidant, which ends in removal. No surprises, The standing principle that a bad fact is delivered early, always. The two-year rule, The minimum tenure that reads as stability, and the time required to be trusted completely.
